short.q: Define solubility.
short.hi: Solubility = saturated solution में घुले solute की मात्रा; IP terms parts of solvent पर

kp.t: Very soluble: less than 1 part solvent

short.a:
Solubility is the concentration of solute in a saturated solution at a definite temperature, i.e. when solute and solvent are in equilibrium.
Pharmacopoeial terms (parts of solvent for 1 part of solute):
Very soluble: less than 1
Freely soluble: 1-10
Soluble: 10-30
Sparingly soluble: 30-100
Slightly soluble: 100-1000
Very slightly soluble: 1000-10,000
Practically insoluble: more than 10,000.

short.q: Write the different ways of expressing the concentration (solubility) of a solution.
short.hi: Molarity, molality, mole fraction, % w/v, normality

kp.t: Molarity: moles per litre of solution
Molality: moles per kg of solvent

short.a:
Solubility/concentration can be expressed as:
1. Molarity (M): moles of solute per litre of solution.
2. Molality (m): moles of solute per 1000 g (1 kg) of solvent; not affected by temperature.
3. Normality (N): gram equivalent weights of solute per litre of solution.
4. Mole fraction: moles of one component divided by total moles of all components.
5. Percentage: % w/w, % w/v and % v/v.
6. Parts of solvent required to dissolve 1 part of solute (pharmacopoeial terms).

short.q: Explain the role of polar, non-polar and semi-polar solvents in solute-solvent interaction.
short.hi: Like dissolves like; polar solvent = high dielectric constant + hydrogen bond

kp.t: Polar solvents: high dielectric constant, H-bonding
Non-polar solvents: van der Waals / induced dipole
Semi-polar solvents induce polarity, act as intermediate

short.a:
Solubility depends on 'like dissolves like'.
Polar solvents (water): have high dielectric constant, break covalent bonds of strong electrolytes, solvate ions by ion-dipole forces and form hydrogen bonds with solutes (e.g. alcohols, amines).
Non-polar solvents (hexane, benzene): low dielectric constant; dissolve non-polar solutes by weak van der Waals (London/induced dipole) forces, e.g. oils and fats.
Semi-polar solvents (acetone, alcohol): induce some polarity in non-polar molecules and act as intermediate solvents to mix polar and non-polar liquids, e.g. acetone increases miscibility of ether in water.

short.q: What is an ideal solution?
short.hi: Ideal solution: mixing पर heat या volume change नहीं, Raoult's law follow करता है

kp.t: Obeys Raoult's law at all concentrations
No heat absorbed or evolved on mixing

short.a:
An ideal solution is one in which the forces between unlike molecules (A-B) are equal to those between like molecules (A-A, B-B). Therefore:
1. It obeys Raoult's law over the whole concentration range (pA = pA° XA).
2. There is no heat change (ΔH mixing = 0) and no volume change on mixing (volumes are additive).
3. Properties of the components do not change except by dilution.
Example: benzene and toluene, n-hexane and n-heptane.

short.q: Define solubility parameter. Give its significance.
short.hi: Hildebrand solubility parameter δ = cohesive energy density का square root

kp.t: δ = square root of cohesive energy density
Similar δ values give higher solubility / miscibility

short.a:
Solubility parameter (δ), introduced by Hildebrand, is the square root of the cohesive energy density (internal pressure) of a liquid:
δ = [(ΔHv - RT)/V]^1/2
where ΔHv = heat of vaporization, V = molar volume.
Significance: it measures intermolecular attraction. Solute and solvent with similar δ values mix well and give higher solubility (regular solution theory). It is used to predict solubility of drugs, choose solvents and co-solvent blends, and estimate miscibility of liquids and polymers.

short.q: Write a note on solvation and association.
short.hi: Solvation = solvent molecules solute को घेरते हैं; association = solute molecules आपस में जुड़ते हैं
short.a:
Solvation is the attachment of solvent molecules to solute molecules or ions by ion-dipole, dipole-dipole or hydrogen bonding; in water it is called hydration. Solvation releases energy that helps break the crystal lattice and increases solubility.
Association is the combination of solute molecules with each other, e.g. benzoic acid forms dimers in benzene, and surfactants form micelles. Association changes the effective molecular weight and affects solubility, colligative properties and the distribution coefficient (deviation from the distribution law).

short.q: What is the common ion effect on solubility? Give an example.
short.hi: Common ion डालने से sparingly soluble salt की solubility घटती है

kp.t: Adding a common ion decreases solubility

short.a: The solubility of a sparingly soluble electrolyte decreases when a soluble salt having a common ion is added, because the ionic product must not exceed the solubility product (Ksp), so the equilibrium shifts towards the undissolved salt. Example: solubility of AgCl decreases in NaCl solution; hydrochloride salts of drugs are less soluble in gastric fluid (rich in Cl-).

short.q: What is an azeotrope? Give examples.
short.hi: Azeotrope: constant boiling mixture, simple distillation से अलग नहीं होता

kp.t: Vapour has same composition as liquid
Cannot be separated by fractional distillation

short.a:
An azeotrope is a liquid mixture of definite composition that boils at a constant temperature and gives vapour of the same composition as the liquid, so it cannot be separated by simple or fractional distillation.
Minimum-boiling azeotropes form with large positive deviation from Raoult's law, e.g. ethanol-water (about 95.6% ethanol).
Maximum-boiling azeotropes form with negative deviation, e.g. hydrochloric acid-water (about 20.2% HCl).

short.q: What are conjugate solutions? Explain with an example.
short.hi: Conjugate solutions: partially miscible liquids की दो saturated layers

kp.t: Each layer is a saturated solution of one in the other
Compositions joined by a tie line

short.a:
When two partially miscible liquids are mixed beyond their mutual solubility, they separate into two liquid layers in equilibrium. Each layer is a saturated solution of one liquid in the other; these two layers are called conjugate solutions (conjugate phases).
Example: phenol-water at room temperature gives an upper water-rich layer (phenol dissolved in water) and a lower phenol-rich layer (water dissolved in phenol). Their compositions at a given temperature lie at the two ends of a tie line on the phase diagram.

short.q: Define partition coefficient. What is its significance?
short.hi: Partition coefficient = oil phase concentration / water phase concentration

kp.t: Ratio of concentration in oil and water phases
K = Co/Cw at equilibrium, constant temperature

short.a:
Partition coefficient (K or P) is the ratio of the equilibrium concentration of a solute in the oil (organic, usually n-octanol) phase to that in the aqueous phase at constant temperature: K = Co / Cw. It is usually expressed as log P.
Significance: it measures lipophilicity of a drug; drugs with suitable (moderately high) log P cross lipid membranes easily, so it predicts absorption, distribution and CNS entry. It is also used in extraction, preservative efficacy in emulsions and in QSAR.

short.q: What is Critical Solution Temperature? Explain with the example of the phenol-water system and its applications.
short.hi: Phenol-water: dome curve, upper CST लगभग 66.8°C

kp.t: CST: above it liquids completely miscible
Tie line gives compositions of phases

a.intro: Critical solution temperature (CST) is the temperature at which two partially miscible liquids become completely miscible in all proportions. Phenol-water is the classic example with an upper CST.
points: At room temperature, phenol and water mix only partly and form two conjugate layers: a water-rich layer and a phenol-rich layer.
On heating, phenol dissolves more in water and water more in phenol, so the compositions of the two layers come closer.
The compositions of the two layers at any temperature are read from the ends of a horizontal tie line.
At about 66.8°C (near 34% w/w phenol) the two layers merge into one; this is the upper CST. Above it the system is a single phase at all compositions.
Applications: CST is very sensitive to impurities (e.g. water in phenol, salts), so it is used for purity testing; it guides blending of liquids and formulation of clear phenol/cresol preparations.
a.diagram: Temperature (y-axis) vs % w/w phenol (x-axis): dome-shaped curve; inside = two phases, outside = one phase; horizontal tie line inside; top of dome labelled 'upper CST 66.8°C'.
a.conclusion: Phenol-water shows how temperature controls miscibility, and its CST is a useful purity test.

short.q: Define CST and explain the different types of partially miscible systems with suitable examples.
short.hi: Upper CST (phenol-water), lower CST (triethylamine-water), दोनों (nicotine-water)

kp.t: Both upper and lower CST: nicotine-water

a.intro: Critical solution temperature (consolute temperature) is the temperature above or below which two partially miscible liquids become miscible in all proportions. Partially miscible systems are of three types.
points: Systems with upper CST: mutual solubility increases with rise in temperature and the liquids become completely miscible above the CST. Example: phenol-water (about 66.8°C), aniline-water.
Systems with lower CST: mutual solubility increases as temperature falls; the liquids are completely miscible below the lower CST and separate into two layers above it. Example: triethylamine-water.
Systems with both upper and lower CST: miscible below the lower CST and above the upper CST, partially miscible in between. Example: nicotine-water; the curve is a closed loop.
Systems with no CST: e.g. ether-water, which remain partially miscible over the accessible temperature range.
a.diagram: Three small graphs of temperature vs composition: (a) dome with maximum (upper CST), (b) inverted dome with minimum (lower CST), (c) closed oval loop (both CSTs).
a.conclusion: The type of curve tells the formulator in which temperature range two liquids will remain a single clear phase.

short.q: State Raoult's law for ideal solutions. Briefly explain how positive and negative deviations occur in real solutions and the types of intermolecular forces involved.
short.hi: Raoult's law: pA = pA°XA; deviation = adhesive vs cohesive forces का अंतर

kp.t: Positive deviation: weaker A-B forces, higher vapour pressure
Negative deviation: stronger A-B forces (H-bonding), lower vapour pressure

a.intro: Raoult's law: in an ideal solution the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component equals the vapour pressure of the pure component multiplied by its mole fraction: pA = pA° XA; total P = pA + pB.
points: Real solutions deviate because the attractive (adhesive) forces between unlike molecules A-B are not equal to the cohesive forces A-A and B-B.

Positive deviation: A-B attraction is weaker than A-A and B-B (e.g. a polar liquid mixed with a non-polar one, where H-bonds/dipole interactions of one component are broken). Molecules escape easily, so vapour pressure is higher than predicted; heat is absorbed and volume expands. Example: benzene-ethanol, carbon disulfide-acetone. Large positive deviation gives minimum-boiling azeotropes or partial miscibility.

Negative deviation: A-B attraction is stronger, usually due to hydrogen bonding or dipole-dipole interaction between unlike molecules. Vapour pressure is lower than predicted; heat is evolved and volume contracts. Example: chloroform-acetone (H-bond between CHCl3 hydrogen and C=O oxygen). May give maximum-boiling azeotropes.
Intermolecular forces involved: hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole (Keesom), dipole-induced dipole (Debye) and London dispersion forces.
a.diagram: Vapour pressure vs mole fraction: straight dashed line for ideal; curve above it for positive deviation; curve below it for negative deviation.
a.conclusion: Whether a mixture deviates positively or negatively depends on how strongly its unlike molecules attract each other.

short.q: Give any two examples of eutectic mixtures.
short.hi: Eutectic: सबसे कम melting point वाला mixture, e.g. camphor-menthol

kp.t: Lowest melting mixture, below either component
Importance: liquefaction in dispensing, solid dispersions

short.a:
A eutectic mixture is a mixture of two components in a definite ratio that melts at a temperature lower than the melting point of either component (eutectic point).
Examples: camphor-menthol, menthol-thymol, camphor-salol, lidocaine-prilocaine (EMLA cream).
Importance: explains liquefaction of some powder mixtures during dispensing; used to make solid dispersions that improve dissolution and to prepare local anaesthetic creams.

short.q: Define polymorphism.
short.hi: Polymorphism: एक ही drug के अलग-अलग crystal forms

kp.t: Same compound exists in more than one crystal form
Different physical properties: melting point, solubility

short.a:
Polymorphism is the ability of a substance to exist in more than one crystalline form, having the same chemical composition but different arrangement of molecules in the crystal lattice. Polymorphs differ in melting point, density, solubility, dissolution rate, stability and bioavailability.
Examples: chloramphenicol palmitate (form B is better absorbed than form A), cocoa butter (α, β', β forms).

short.q: Name any two physicochemical properties of drug molecules.
short.hi: Refractive index, optical rotation, dielectric constant, dipole moment, pKa
short.a:
Physicochemical properties of drug molecules (any two):
1. Refractive index - ratio of velocity of light in vacuum to that in the substance; used for identification and purity.
2. Optical rotation - rotation of plane-polarised light by chiral molecules.
3. Dielectric constant and dipole moment - measure polarity.
4. Dissociation constant (pKa) - extent of ionisation.

short.q: Write the difference between amorphous and crystalline solids.
short.hi: Crystalline: ordered lattice, sharp m.p.; amorphous: random, no sharp m.p.

kp.t: Crystalline: sharp melting point; amorphous melts over a range

short.a:
Crystalline solids: atoms/molecules arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional lattice; sharp melting point; anisotropic; definite heat of fusion; more stable, less soluble. Example: NaCl, sucrose.
Amorphous solids: random arrangement (no long-range order); soften and melt over a range (glass transition); isotropic; higher energy, more soluble and faster dissolving but less stable. Example: glass, amorphous novobiocin.

short.q: Define latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization.
short.hi: Latent heat: state change पर बिना temperature बदले absorbed heat

kp.t: Heat absorbed at constant temperature during change of state
Fusion: solid to liquid at melting point
Vaporization: liquid to vapour at boiling point

short.a:
Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released when a substance changes its state at constant temperature.
Latent heat of fusion: heat required to convert 1 g (or 1 mole) of a solid into liquid at its melting point without temperature change (ice: about 80 cal/g or 334 J/g).
Latent heat of vaporization: heat required to convert 1 g of liquid into vapour at its boiling point (water: about 540 cal/g or 2257 J/g at 100°C).

short.q: Define vapour pressure. How does temperature affect it?
short.hi: Vapour pressure: liquid के ऊपर equilibrium vapour का pressure; temperature बढ़े तो बढ़ता है

kp.t: Pressure of vapour in equilibrium with liquid
Boiling when VP equals external pressure

short.a:
Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour in equilibrium with its liquid (or solid) at a given temperature in a closed container.
It increases with temperature because more molecules gain enough energy to escape; the relation is given by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation: log(p2/p1) = ΔHv (T2 - T1)/(2.303 R T1 T2). A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

short.q: What is glass transition temperature (Tg)?
short.hi: Tg: इस temperature पर amorphous solid glassy से rubbery बनता है

kp.t: Temperature at which amorphous solid changes glassy to rubbery
Applies to amorphous solids and polymers
Below Tg hard and brittle; above Tg mobile, less stable

short.a: Glass transition temperature (Tg) is the temperature at which an amorphous solid or polymer changes from a hard, brittle glassy state to a soft, rubbery (more mobile) state. Below Tg molecular mobility is very low and the material is physically stable; above Tg mobility increases, which can lead to crystallisation and chemical instability. Water acts as a plasticizer and lowers Tg.

short.q: Define specific rotation and give its formula.
short.hi: Specific rotation = 100α / (l × c)

kp.t: Rotation by 1 dm tube, 1 g/mL concentration
Specified temperature and wavelength (sodium D line)

short.a:
Specific rotation [α] is the angle of rotation of plane-polarised light produced by a solution containing 1 g of substance per mL in a 1 dm tube, at a specified temperature and wavelength (usually 20 or 25°C, sodium D line 589 nm).
[α] = 100 α / (l × c)
α = observed rotation, l = path length in dm, c = concentration in g/100 mL. Dextrorotatory (+), laevorotatory (-).

short.q: Define dielectric constant. Give the dielectric constant of water.
short.hi: Dielectric constant = C / C0; water ≈ 78.5 at 25°C

kp.t: Ratio of capacitance with substance to vacuum
Measure of polarity / ability to separate charges

short.a: Dielectric constant (ε) is the ratio of the capacitance of a condenser with the substance between its plates (C) to its capacitance with vacuum (C0): ε = C / C0. It indicates the polarity of a solvent and its ability to reduce the attraction between oppositely charged ions. Water has a high dielectric constant of about 78.5 at 25°C, so it dissolves electrolytes well.

short.q: Define dissociation constant and pKa.
short.hi: Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA]; pKa = -log Ka
short.a: Dissociation constant (Ka) is the equilibrium constant for ionisation of a weak acid: HA + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + A-, Ka = [H3O+][A-]/[HA]. pKa = -log Ka. pKa is the pH at which the drug is 50% ionised; a lower pKa means a stronger acid. For bases the pKa of the conjugate acid is used.

short.q: Explain the concept of eutectic mixtures with a cooling curve diagram and provide their applications in formulation design.
short.hi: Eutectic point पर दोनों solids साथ में crystallise होते हैं

kp.t: Mixture with lowest melting point at fixed composition
Phase diagram: V-shaped with eutectic point
Cooling curve: halt (flat) at eutectic temperature

a.intro: A eutectic mixture is a mixture of two (or more) solids, completely miscible in the liquid state but immiscible in the solid state, which at a definite composition melts at the lowest temperature of all possible mixtures (the eutectic point).
points: Phase diagram: temperature vs composition. Each pure component's melting point falls when the other is added; the two liquidus curves meet at the lowest point, the eutectic point.
Above the liquidus curves: single liquid phase. Between liquidus and eutectic line: one solid in equilibrium with liquid. Below the eutectic temperature: two solid phases.
At the eutectic point the liquid freezes at a single temperature into an intimate mixture of fine crystals of both components (F = 0 at constant pressure).

Cooling curve: when a molten mixture is cooled, temperature falls smoothly until one component starts to crystallise (change in slope, a 'break'); for the eutectic composition the curve shows no break but a single horizontal halt (plateau) at the eutectic temperature, like a pure substance, until all the liquid has solidified. Pure components also show a single halt at their own melting points.
Examples: thymol-salol, camphor-menthol, menthol-thymol, lidocaine-prilocaine.

Applications in formulation design: (a) eutectic formation explains liquefaction or dampness of some powder mixtures in dispensing (e.g. camphor-menthol); (b) EMLA cream (eutectic of lidocaine and prilocaine) for topical anaesthesia; (c) solid dispersions/eutectics of poorly soluble drugs with carriers (e.g. griseofulvin-succinic acid) increase dissolution and bioavailability; (d) purity determination.
a.diagram: Draw (1) cooling curves: temperature (y) vs time (x) for pure A (one flat halt), a non-eutectic mixture (a break then a halt at the eutectic temperature) and the eutectic mixture (single halt at the lowest temperature); (2) the phase diagram built from these: two liquidus curves meeting at eutectic point E, with regions liquid, liquid + A, liquid + B, solid A + solid B.
a.conclusion: Eutectics are both a dispensing problem and a useful tool to improve dissolution of drugs.

short.q: Discuss the determination and pharmaceutical applications of refractive index.
short.hi: n = sin i / sin r; Abbe refractometer

kp.t: n = sin i / sin r (or c vacuum / c medium)
Depends on temperature and wavelength (sodium D line)

a.intro: Refractive index (n) is the ratio of the velocity of light in vacuum (or air) to its velocity in the substance. By Snell's law, n = sin i / sin r, where i = angle of incidence, r = angle of refraction.
points: n depends on temperature and wavelength; it is usually reported at 20°C with the sodium D line (589 nm), written n20D.

Determination: Abbe refractometer works on the critical angle principle. A few drops of liquid are placed between two prisms; light passes, the instrument is adjusted until the field shows a sharp boundary between light and dark halves on the cross-wires, and n is read directly from the scale. Compensator prisms remove colour fringes. Temperature is controlled by water circulation.
Molar refraction Rm = [(n² - 1)/(n² + 2)] × (M/ρ) (Lorentz-Lorenz equation) is an additive, constitutive property related to polarizability.

Applications: identification and purity testing of oils, solvents and essential oils (pharmacopoeial standard); determination of concentration of solutions (e.g. sugar solutions); detection of adulteration; calculation of molar refraction and polarizability for structure study.
a.diagram: Abbe refractometer: light source/mirror, illuminating and refracting prisms with sample between, compensator (Amici prisms), telescope with cross-wires, and scale.
a.conclusion: Refractive index is a quick, non-destructive test of identity, purity and concentration.

short.q: Differentiate between crystalline and amorphous solids and write a short note on the importance of polymorphism in drug formulation.
short.hi: Crystalline vs amorphous + polymorphism: enantiotropic/monotropic

kp.t: Amorphous: random, glass transition, more soluble
Polymorphism: different crystal forms, same compound

a.intro: Solids are classified as crystalline (regular, repeating arrangement of units) and amorphous (random arrangement without long-range order).
points: Crystalline solids: have a unit cell repeated in three dimensions; seven crystal systems (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal, trigonal); sharp melting point, anisotropic, lower energy and lower solubility; studied by X-ray diffraction.

Amorphous solids: random arrangement like a frozen liquid; no sharp melting point (show glass transition, Tg); isotropic; higher free energy, so higher solubility and faster dissolution but tend to crystallise on storage (e.g. amorphous novobiocin is active, the crystalline form is poorly absorbed).
Polymorphism: the ability of a compound to crystallise in more than one crystal form. Polymorphs differ in melting point, solubility, density, stability and bioavailability.

Enantiotropic polymorphs convert reversibly at a transition temperature (e.g. sulfur); monotropic polymorphs - only one form is stable at all temperatures, the metastable form changes irreversibly to it.

Pharmaceutical importance: chloramphenicol palmitate form B gives higher blood levels than form A; cocoa butter (theobroma oil) must be melted gently to avoid unstable forms in suppositories; polymorphs are characterised by XRD, DSC, IR and hot-stage microscopy.
a.conclusion: The solid form chosen for a drug affects its solubility, stability and bioavailability, so it must be controlled.

short.q: Define relative humidity. Explain its measurement and pharmaceutical significance, including critical relative humidity.
short.hi: RH = (partial pressure of water vapour / saturated VP) × 100

kp.t: RH = partial pressure / saturation vapour pressure × 100
Measured by hygrometer / wet and dry bulb

a.intro: Relative humidity (RH) is the ratio of the partial pressure of water vapour in air to the saturated vapour pressure of water at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage.
points: RH = (p / p0) × 100, where p = actual partial pressure of water vapour, p0 = saturated vapour pressure at that temperature.
Measurement: wet and dry bulb hygrometer (psychrometer) - difference between the two readings is used with tables; dew point hygrometer; hair hygrometer; electronic (capacitance) sensors.

Critical relative humidity (CRH): the RH at which a water-soluble solid begins to absorb moisture from the air significantly. Above CRH the solid picks up water and may deliquesce (dissolve in the absorbed water), e.g. calcium chloride.
The CRH of a mixture of water-soluble salts is lower than that of either component, so mixtures absorb moisture more easily.

Significance: hygroscopic and deliquescent drugs must be manufactured and stored below their CRH; RH affects granule moisture, tablet hardness, capsule shell brittleness or softening, powder flow, chemical stability (hydrolysis) and microbial growth; it guides choice of packaging and desiccants and controls drying operations.
a.diagram: Graph: moisture uptake (y) vs RH (x) showing near-zero uptake up to CRH then a sharp rise.
a.conclusion: Controlling humidity below the critical value protects moisture-sensitive drugs and dosage forms.

short.q: Explain sublimation and critical point with the help of the phase diagram of water.
short.hi: Triple point, sublimation curve, critical point (374°C, 218 atm)

kp.t: Critical temperature: gas cannot be liquefied above it

a.intro: The phase diagram of water shows the conditions of temperature and pressure at which ice, water and vapour exist and are in equilibrium.
points: Three curves: fusion (solid-liquid), vaporization (liquid-vapour) and sublimation (solid-vapour); they meet at the triple point (0.0098°C, 4.58 mm Hg) where all three phases coexist (F = 0).

Sublimation: direct change of a solid into vapour without melting; occurs when the pressure is below the triple point pressure. Examples: camphor, iodine, naphthalene, menthol. Freeze drying (lyophilisation) removes ice by sublimation under vacuum for heat-sensitive products like antibiotics and vaccines.

Critical point: the end of the vaporization curve. Critical temperature is the temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied however high the pressure; critical pressure is the pressure needed to liquefy the gas at the critical temperature. For water about 374°C and 218 atm.
Above the critical point the substance is a supercritical fluid; supercritical CO2 (critical point about 31°C, 73 atm) is used for extraction of natural products and particle engineering.
Knowledge of critical temperature is used in liquefaction of gases such as aerosol propellants.
a.diagram: Phase diagram of water: pressure (y) vs temperature (x); curve OA (vapour pressure of liquid) ending at critical point A; curve OB (sublimation); line OC (fusion) slightly tilted to the left; O = triple point; regions labelled ice, water, vapour.
a.conclusion: Sublimation is the basis of freeze drying and the critical point is the basis of supercritical fluid technology.

short.q: What is optical rotation? Describe the polarimeter and give applications of optical rotation.
short.hi: Polarimeter: polarizer + sample tube + analyzer; [α] = 100α/lc

kp.t: Rotation of plane-polarised light by chiral molecules
Polarimeter: polarizer, sample tube, analyzer (Nicol prisms)

a.intro: Optical rotation is the property of optically active (chiral) substances to rotate the plane of plane-polarised light. Rotation to the right (clockwise) is dextrorotatory (+), to the left laevorotatory (-).
points: Polarimeter: monochromatic light source (sodium lamp, 589 nm) → polarizer (Nicol prism) gives plane-polarised light → sample tube (usually 1 or 2 dm) containing the solution → analyzer (second Nicol prism) attached to a graduated circular scale → eyepiece.

Working: with the empty/solvent tube the analyzer is set for darkness (or equal half-shade); with the sample in place, the analyzer is rotated to restore the same field; the angle turned is the observed rotation α.
Specific rotation: [α] = 100 α / (l × c), where l = tube length in dm, c = g/100 mL; reported at a stated temperature and wavelength.

Applications: identification and purity of optically active drugs (e.g. sugars, camphor, alkaloids); assay of concentration (e.g. dextrose injection); study of racemisation and reaction kinetics (inversion of sucrose); distinguishing enantiomers that differ in activity.
a.diagram: Polarimeter diagram: sodium lamp → polarizer prism → sample tube → analyzer prism with circular scale → eyepiece.
a.conclusion: Optical rotation is a simple, specific test for chiral drugs used in pharmacopoeial monographs.

short.q: Write the full form of HLB.
short.hi: HLB = Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance (Griffin scale)

kp.t: Balance of polar and non-polar groups of surfactant

short.a: HLB stands for Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance (hydrophile-lipophile balance). It is an arbitrary scale introduced by Griffin that expresses the balance between the water-loving (polar) and oil-loving (non-polar) parts of a surfactant molecule. Low HLB = lipophilic; high HLB = hydrophilic.

short.q: What is surface free energy?
short.hi: Surface बढ़ाने के लिए किया गया work = surface free energy

kp.t: Work required to increase surface by unit area

short.a: Surface free energy is the work required to increase the surface area of a liquid by unit area (1 cm²) against the inward pull of surface molecules. W = γ × ΔA, where γ is the surface tension. It is expressed in erg/cm² (numerically equal to surface tension in dyne/cm) or J/m².

short.q: Define critical micelle concentration (CMC).
short.hi: CMC: जिस concentration पर surfactant micelle बनाना शुरू करता है

kp.t: Concentration at which micelles start to form
Sudden change in physical properties (surface tension, conductivity)

short.a: Critical micelle concentration (CMC) is the concentration of a surfactant at which its molecules start to aggregate to form micelles in solution. Above CMC the surface is saturated with surfactant, so surface tension stays nearly constant, and properties such as conductivity, osmotic pressure and light scattering change abruptly. Solubilisation begins above the CMC.

short.q: Classify surface active agents with examples.
short.hi: Anionic, cationic, non-ionic, ampholytic surfactants
short.a:
Surfactants are classified by the charge on their hydrophilic group:
1. Anionic - sodium lauryl sulphate, sodium stearate (soaps).
2. Cationic - benzalkonium chloride, cetrimide (quaternary ammonium compounds).
3. Non-ionic - sorbitan esters (Spans), polysorbates (Tweens).
4. Ampholytic (zwitterionic) - lecithin, N-dodecyl alanine.

short.q: Write the Freundlich adsorption isotherm and explain its terms.
short.hi: x/m = k c^(1/n); log form straight line

kp.t: x = amount adsorbed, m = mass of adsorbent
log x/m = log k + (1/n) log c, straight line

short.a:
Freundlich adsorption isotherm: x/m = k c^(1/n)
x = amount of gas/solute adsorbed, m = mass of adsorbent, c = equilibrium concentration (or pressure p for gases), k and n are constants (n > 1).
Taking logs: log(x/m) = log k + (1/n) log c, so a plot of log(x/m) vs log c is a straight line with slope 1/n and intercept log k. It is empirical and fails at high pressure.

short.q: What is contact angle? Give its significance in wetting.
short.hi: Contact angle कम = wetting अच्छी

kp.t: Angle between liquid surface and solid at contact point
Importance in granulation, dissolution, wetting agents

short.a: Contact angle (θ) is the angle between the surface of a liquid drop and the solid surface at the point where liquid, solid and air meet. θ = 0° means complete wetting (spreading), θ < 90° partial wetting, θ > 90° poor wetting, 180° no wetting. Hydrophobic powders (high θ) need wetting agents in suspensions; contact angle affects granulation, dissolution and penetration of liquids into tablets.

short.q: Define interfacial tension. How does it differ from surface tension?
short.hi: Interfacial tension: दो immiscible liquids के बीच का tension

kp.t: Force per unit length at interface of two immiscible phases
Units dyne/cm; interfacial tension usually lower

short.a: Interfacial tension is the force per unit length existing at the interface between two immiscible liquid phases (e.g. oil and water), measured in dyne/cm. Surface tension is the same force at a liquid-air (liquid-vapour) interface. Interfacial tension is usually lower than the larger of the two surface tensions because adhesive forces between the two liquids partly balance the cohesive forces.

short.q: Describe the Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance (HLB) scale and its role in selecting the appropriate surfactant for various pharmaceutical systems.
short.hi: HLB 1-3 antifoam, 3-6 w/o, 7-9 wetting, 8-18 o/w, 13-15 detergent, 15-18 solubiliser

kp.t: Low HLB lipophilic, high HLB hydrophilic

a.intro: The HLB (hydrophilic-lipophilic balance) scale, introduced by Griffin, is an arbitrary numerical scale (mostly 1-20 for non-ionic surfactants) that expresses the balance between the hydrophilic and lipophilic parts of a surfactant. Higher HLB = more hydrophilic.
points: Applications by HLB range: 1-3 antifoaming agents; 3-6 w/o emulsifying agents; 7-9 wetting agents; 8-18 o/w emulsifying agents; 13-15 detergents; 15-18 solubilising agents.
Examples: Span 80 (sorbitan monooleate) HLB 4.3 - w/o emulsifier; Tween 80 (polysorbate 80) HLB 15 - o/w emulsifier and solubiliser; sodium lauryl sulphate about 40 (Davies scale).

Calculation (Griffin): for polyhydric alcohol fatty acid esters HLB = 20(1 - S/A), S = saponification value of ester, A = acid number of fatty acid; for ethylene oxide-only hydrophilic groups HLB = E/5 (E = weight % oxyethylene). Davies: HLB = Σ hydrophilic group numbers - Σ lipophilic group numbers + 7.
HLB of a blend = (fraction A × HLB A) + (fraction B × HLB B); blends of a Span and a Tween are used to match the 'required HLB' of the oil phase for a stable emulsion.
Limitations: it does not consider temperature, concentration or the chemical nature of the oil.
a.diagram: Draw a vertical HLB scale from 0 to 20 with bands labelled: antifoam (1-3), w/o emulsifier (3-6), wetting agent (7-9), o/w emulsifier (8-18), detergent (13-15), solubiliser (15-18).
a.conclusion: HLB guides selection of surfactants for emulsions, wetting, detergency and solubilisation.

short.q: Define spreading coefficient. Derive it from work of adhesion and work of cohesion and give its significance.
short.hi: S = Wa - Wc; S positive हो तो liquid spread करेगा

kp.t: Work of adhesion Wa = γL + γS - γLS
Positive S: spreads; negative S: forms lens
Significance: lotions, wetting of skin, film coating

a.intro: When a liquid is placed on another liquid or on a solid, it may spread as a film or remain as a drop (lens). The tendency to spread is expressed by the spreading coefficient (S).
points: Work of adhesion (Wa): energy required to separate unit area of the interface between two different substances: Wa = γS + γL - γSL.
Work of cohesion (Wc): energy required to separate unit area of a single liquid into two surfaces: Wc = 2γL.
Spreading coefficient: S = Wa - Wc = (γS + γL - γSL) - 2γL = γS - (γL + γSL); here S = sublayer (substrate), L = spreading liquid.
If S is positive (adhesion > cohesion), the liquid spreads over the surface as a film; if S is negative, it remains as a globule or lens.
Example: oleic acid, which has a polar COOH group, spreads on water; liquid paraffin (non-polar) does not. Mutual saturation of the liquids reduces S, so initial spreading may stop later.
Significance: spreading of lotions and ointments on skin (skin is non-polar, surfactants aid spreading), film coating of tablets, wetting of powders, design of insecticidal and cosmetic sprays.
a.diagram: Draw a drop of oil on water: (a) spreading as a thin film (S positive), (b) a lens with interfacial tensions γO, γW, γOW shown as arrows at the edge (S negative).
a.conclusion: A positive spreading coefficient means good spreading and is desired for topical products and coatings.

short.q: Explain adsorption at liquid interfaces. Derive the significance of the Gibbs adsorption equation.
short.hi: Gibbs equation: Γ = -(c/RT)(dγ/dc); surfactant positive adsorption

kp.t: Adsorption: higher concentration at the interface than bulk
Positive adsorption: surfactants lower surface tension
Negative adsorption: electrolytes raise surface tension
Orientation: polar head in water, tail in air/oil

a.intro: Adsorption at a liquid interface is the accumulation of a solute at the surface (or interface) at a concentration different from that in the bulk solution. Amphiphilic molecules adsorb strongly at liquid-air and liquid-liquid interfaces.
points: Surface active agents have a polar head and non-polar tail; at the interface they orient with the polar group in water and the hydrocarbon tail towards air or oil, forming a monolayer.
Positive adsorption: solutes (surfactants, alcohols, fatty acids) concentrate at the surface and lower surface tension.
Negative adsorption: inorganic electrolytes and sugars are depleted at the surface and slightly increase surface tension.

Gibbs adsorption equation: Γ = -(c/RT)(dγ/dc), where Γ = surface excess (moles per unit area), c = bulk concentration, dγ/dc = change of surface tension with concentration. If dγ/dc is negative, Γ is positive (positive adsorption).
From the slope of γ vs log c just below the CMC, Γ and the area occupied per surfactant molecule at the surface can be calculated.
Importance: explains action of emulsifying agents, wetting agents, foaming agents and the formation of interfacial films around emulsion droplets.
a.diagram: Draw a beaker of water with surfactant molecules shown as circles (head) with tails: heads in water, tails pointing to air at the surface; micelles inside the bulk.
a.conclusion: Adsorption at liquid interfaces, described by the Gibbs equation, is the basis of surfactant action.

short.q: What is a chelate? Give two examples of chelating agents used in therapy.
short.hi: Chelate: multidentate ligand metal के साथ ring बनाता है

kp.t: Ligand with two or more donor atoms forms ring with metal
EDTA (calcium disodium edetate) for lead poisoning

short.a:
A chelate is a complex in which a ligand having two or more donor atoms (multidentate ligand) binds a single metal ion at more than one site, forming a stable ring (usually 5- or 6-membered).
Therapeutic chelating agents: calcium disodium EDTA (lead poisoning), dimercaprol/BAL (arsenic, mercury, gold), desferrioxamine (iron overload), penicillamine (copper in Wilson's disease).

short.q: What are cyclodextrins? Give their use in complexation.
short.hi: Cyclodextrin: glucose का cyclic ring, inside hydrophobic cavity

kp.t: Cyclic oligosaccharides of glucose (α-6, β-7, γ-8 units)

short.a: Cyclodextrins are cyclic oligosaccharides made of glucose units: α-cyclodextrin (6), β-cyclodextrin (7) and γ-cyclodextrin (8). They are cone-shaped with a hydrophobic inner cavity and a hydrophilic outer surface. A lipophilic drug enters the cavity to form a monomolecular inclusion complex, which increases aqueous solubility, dissolution and stability, masks bitter taste and reduces irritation (e.g. piroxicam-β-cyclodextrin).

short.q: What are clathrates? Give an example.
short.hi: Clathrate: host की cage-like lattice में guest molecule फँसा रहता है

kp.t: Guest trapped in cage-like crystal lattice of host
No chemical bond; size of guest important

short.a:
Clathrates are inclusion compounds in which guest molecules are trapped in cage-like cavities of the crystal lattice of a host compound, without chemical bonding; the size and shape of the guest decide whether it fits.
Examples: hydroquinone (quinol) crystallises with cavities that trap methanol, SO2 or HCl; warfarin sodium is available as a clathrate with isopropyl alcohol.

short.q: Define stability constant of a complex.
short.hi: Stability constant K बड़ा = complex ज़्यादा stable
short.a: Stability constant (formation constant) is the equilibrium constant for formation of a complex from metal (or substrate) M and ligand A: M + A ⇌ MA, K = [MA]/([M][A]). The larger the value of K, the more stable the complex. It is related to free energy change: ΔG° = -2.303 RT log K. For stepwise complexes the overall constant β = K1 × K2 × ... Kn.

short.q: Name the plasma proteins that bind drugs, with examples of drugs bound.
short.hi: Albumin: acidic drugs; α1-acid glycoprotein: basic drugs

kp.t: Albumin binds acidic drugs (warfarin, phenylbutazone, salicylates)
α1-acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs (propranolol, lidocaine)

short.a:
1. Human serum albumin - the most important; binds mainly acidic (anionic) drugs such as warfarin, phenylbutazone, salicylates, sulfonamides, and also some bases.
2. α1-acid glycoprotein (orosomucoid) - binds basic drugs such as propranolol, lidocaine, imipramine.
3. Lipoproteins - bind lipophilic drugs.
4. Globulins - bind specific substances (e.g. corticosteroid-binding globulin for hormones).

short.q: What is drug displacement in protein binding? Give an example.
short.hi: Displacement: strong binder दूसरे drug को albumin से हटाता है, free drug बढ़ता है

kp.t: One drug displaces another from same binding site

short.a:
Drug displacement occurs when two drugs compete for the same binding site on a plasma protein; the drug with higher affinity displaces the other, increasing the free (active) concentration of the displaced drug. It is significant for highly bound drugs with narrow therapeutic index.
Examples: phenylbutazone displaces warfarin from albumin causing bleeding; sulfonamides displace bilirubin in newborns causing kernicterus.

short.q: Define complexation. Write the classification of complexes. Describe the solubility method for the analysis of complexes.
short.hi: Complex classification + Higuchi-Connors phase solubility (A and B type)

kp.t: Complex: association of two or more molecules (donor-acceptor)
Metal ion complexes: inorganic, chelates, olefin, aromatic
Organic molecular complexes: quinhydrone, caffeine, picric acid, polymer
Inclusion compounds: channel, layer, clathrate, cyclodextrin, molecular sieves
Solubility method: excess drug + increasing ligand (Higuchi & Connors)
Type A (AL, AP, AN) and Type B (BS, BI) diagrams

a.intro: Complexation is the reversible association of a substrate (often a metal ion or drug) with one or more ligands (molecules or ions) through coordinate bonds or weaker forces (hydrogen bonds, charge transfer, van der Waals, hydrophobic) to form a new species, the complex.
points: Classification - I. Metal ion complexes: (a) inorganic type, e.g. [Cu(NH3)4]2+; (b) chelates, e.g. EDTA-Ca, Cu-glycinate; (c) olefin type, e.g. ethylene-silver; (d) aromatic type (π complexes with aromatic rings).

II. Organic molecular complexes: quinhydrone (quinone + hydroquinone), picric acid complexes, caffeine and other drug complexes (caffeine with benzocaine, PABA), polymer complexes (PEG, PVP and CMC with drugs).

III. Inclusion or occlusion compounds: channel lattice (urea, thiourea, deoxycholic acid), layer type (montmorillonite clay, graphite), clathrates (hydroquinone), monomolecular inclusion (cyclodextrins), macromolecular (molecular sieves/zeolites, dextrins, silica gel).

Solubility method (Higuchi and Connors): an excess of the drug (substrate) is placed in vials with increasing concentrations of the ligand, shaken at constant temperature until equilibrium, filtered and the total dissolved drug is assayed. Total drug solubility is plotted against ligand concentration (phase solubility diagram).

Type A diagrams (soluble complexes): AL - linear rise (1:1 complex); AP - positive deviation (higher-order complexes); AN - negative deviation. For AL, K(1:1) = slope / [S0 (1 - slope)], S0 = intrinsic solubility.

Type B diagrams (complexes of limited solubility): BS - initial rise, a plateau when the complex's solubility is reached, then fall as solid complex precipitates; BI - insoluble complex, no initial rise. Stoichiometry can be calculated from the plateau region.
a.diagram: Phase solubility diagram: total drug concentration (y) vs ligand concentration (x) with lines AL (straight), AP (curving up), AN (curving down), BS (rise-plateau-fall) and BI (flat-fall).
a.conclusion: The solubility method gives both the stoichiometry and the stability constant of drug complexes.

short.q: Explain the Klotz reciprocal plot and Scatchard plot used in the analysis of protein binding data.
short.hi: Klotz: 1/r vs 1/Df; Scatchard: r/Df vs r

kp.t: r = moles bound per mole protein = nKDf/(1 + KDf)

a.intro: Protein binding data are analysed using the Langmuir-type equation: r = nK[Df]/(1 + K[Df]), where r = moles of drug bound per mole of protein, n = number of binding sites per protein molecule, K = association (binding) constant, Df = free drug concentration.
points: Klotz (double reciprocal) plot: 1/r = 1/(nK Df) + 1/n. A plot of 1/r (y) vs 1/Df (x) is a straight line with intercept 1/n and slope 1/(nK); so n and K are obtained.
Klotz plot is useful when binding is of one class; it is weighted towards low concentrations.
Scatchard plot: rearranging gives r/Df = nK - rK. A plot of r/Df (y) vs r (x) is a straight line with slope -K, y-intercept nK and x-intercept n.
If the Scatchard plot is curved, the protein has more than one class of binding sites (e.g. high-affinity and low-affinity sites).
The free and bound drug concentrations needed for these plots are measured by equilibrium dialysis or ultrafiltration.
a.diagram: Two graphs: (1) Klotz: 1/r vs 1/Df straight line, intercept on y-axis = 1/n; (2) Scatchard: r/Df vs r straight line with negative slope -K, cutting the x-axis at n.
a.conclusion: These plots give the number of binding sites and the affinity constant of a drug for a protein.

short.q: Discuss the pharmaceutical applications of complexation, including complexation and drug action.
short.hi: Solubility, stability, chelation therapy, absorption पर effect

kp.t: Increase solubility (iodine-KI, PVP-iodine, cyclodextrins, caffeine-sodium benzoate)
Biological complexes: haemoglobin, chlorophyll, vitamin B12

a.intro: Complexation changes the solubility, stability, absorption and activity of drugs, and is used deliberately in formulation and therapy.
points: Solubility enhancement: iodine is solubilised by potassium iodide (forming KI3) and by povidone (povidone-iodine); caffeine is made more soluble with sodium benzoate; cyclodextrins form soluble inclusion complexes with poorly soluble drugs.
Stability: caffeine complex reduces hydrolysis of benzocaine and procaine; cyclodextrin inclusion protects drugs from oxidation, hydrolysis and volatilisation.
Antioxidant action: EDTA sequesters trace heavy metal ions that catalyse oxidation and acts as an antioxidant synergist.
Chelation therapy: calcium disodium EDTA for lead, dimercaprol for arsenic and mercury, desferrioxamine for iron, penicillamine for copper.

Complexation and drug action: tetracyclines chelate Ca, Mg, Al and Fe (antacids, milk) and their absorption falls; some drugs act by chelation (e.g. 8-hydroxyquinoline's antimicrobial action); metal complexes in the body (haemoglobin-Fe, chlorophyll-Mg, vitamin B12-Co) are essential.
Others: taste masking, controlled release (drug-resin and polymer complexes), complexometric titrations with EDTA in analysis.
a.conclusion: Complexation is a versatile tool to improve solubility and stability, treat poisoning, and it explains several drug interactions.

short.q: What is a buffer solution?
short.hi: Buffer: थोड़ा acid/base डालने पर pH नहीं बदलता

kp.t: Resists change in pH on adding small acid or base

short.a: A buffer solution is a solution that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added or when it is diluted. It usually consists of a weak acid and its salt (conjugate base), e.g. acetic acid-sodium acetate, or a weak base and its salt, e.g. ammonia-ammonium chloride.

short.q: Define isotonic solution.
short.hi: Isotonic: body fluid जैसा osmotic pressure, जैसे 0.9% NaCl

kp.t: Same osmotic pressure as body fluids (blood, tears)
No swelling or shrinking of RBCs

short.a: An isotonic solution is one that has the same osmotic pressure as body fluids such as blood plasma and lacrimal fluid, so red blood cells placed in it neither swell nor shrink. Example: 0.9% w/v sodium chloride solution; it has the same freezing point depression as blood and tears (-0.52°C).

short.q: Define pH according to Sorensen. What are its limitations?
short.hi: Sorensen: pH = -log[H+]
short.a:
Sorensen (1909) defined pH as the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = -log[H+] = log(1/[H+]). At 25°C, pH + pOH = 14 (pKw). More correctly pH = -log aH+ (activity).
Limitations: it uses concentration instead of activity, so it is inexact for concentrated solutions; values outside 0-14 occur for strong acids/bases; Kw (and the neutral point) changes with temperature.

short.q: Write the buffer equation for a weak base and its salt.
short.hi: pH = pKw - pKb + log [base]/[salt]
short.a:
For a weak base and its salt (e.g. ammonia-ammonium chloride):
pOH = pKb + log [salt]/[base]
Since pH = pKw - pOH:
pH = pKw - pKb + log [base]/[salt]
where pKw = 14 at 25°C and pKb = -log Kb of the base.

short.q: What is the normal pH of blood? Name the buffer systems that maintain it.
short.hi: Blood pH 7.4: bicarbonate, phosphate, protein/haemoglobin buffers
short.a:
The normal pH of blood is about 7.4 (7.35-7.45). It is maintained by:
1. Carbonic acid/bicarbonate system (H2CO3/HCO3-) - the main buffer of plasma.
2. Phosphate system (H2PO4-/HPO4 2-) - important in RBCs and cells.
3. Plasma proteins and haemoglobin/oxyhaemoglobin in red cells.
Lungs and kidneys also regulate pH.

short.q: What is the sodium chloride equivalent (E value)?
short.hi: E value: 1 g drug के बराबर osmotic effect देने वाला NaCl

kp.t: Amount of NaCl equivalent to 1 g of drug
Used to calculate NaCl to make isotonic

short.a: The sodium chloride equivalent (E) of a drug is the amount (g) of sodium chloride that has the same osmotic effect as 1 g of the drug. It is calculated as E = 17 Liso / M (M = molecular weight). It is used to find how much NaCl must be added to make a drug solution isotonic: NaCl needed = 0.9 g per 100 mL - (weight of drug × E).

short.q: Differentiate between hypotonic and hypertonic solutions with respect to RBCs.
short.hi: Hypotonic: RBC फूलकर फटते (hemolysis); hypertonic: सिकुड़ते (crenation)

kp.t: Hypotonic: lower osmotic pressure than body fluids

short.a:
Hypotonic solution: osmotic pressure lower than that of body fluids (less than 0.9% NaCl). Water enters red blood cells, they swell and may burst (haemolysis).
Hypertonic solution: osmotic pressure higher than body fluids (more than 0.9% NaCl). Water leaves the cells, which shrink and become wrinkled (crenation).
Both can cause pain and tissue damage on injection.

short.q: Describe any two methods used to adjust the tonicity of pharmaceutical solutions.
short.hi: Cryoscopic method W = (0.52 - a)/b; NaCl equivalent method

kp.t: Class I methods: add NaCl/solute (cryoscopic, NaCl equivalent)
Class II: White-Vincent V = w × E × 111.1; Sprowls

a.intro: Tonicity is adjusted so that a solution has the same osmotic pressure as body fluids (freezing point depression 0.52°C). Methods are Class I (add a tonicity agent such as NaCl to lower the freezing point to -0.52°C) and Class II (dissolve the drug in enough water to make it isotonic, then dilute with an isotonic vehicle).
points: 1. Cryoscopic (freezing point depression) method: blood and tears freeze at -0.52°C. The weight W (g/100 mL) of adjusting substance needed is W = (0.52 - a)/b, where a = freezing point depression of the unadjusted drug solution and b = freezing point depression of a 1% w/v solution of the adjusting substance (about 0.58 for NaCl).
Example: if a drug solution has a = 0.12, NaCl needed = (0.52 - 0.12)/0.58 ≈ 0.69 g per 100 mL.
2. Sodium chloride equivalent method: E = grams of NaCl equivalent osmotically to 1 g of drug. NaCl to be added (g/100 mL) = 0.9 - Σ(weight of each drug in g × its E value).

Class II methods: White-Vincent method: volume of water V (mL) that makes w g of drug isotonic = w × E × 111.1; the solution is then made up to volume with an isotonic buffered vehicle. Sprowls method uses a table of V values for 0.3 g of drug.
Liso method: ΔTf = Liso × c, used to estimate freezing point depression and E values (E = 17 Liso/M).
a.conclusion: Cryoscopic and NaCl-equivalent methods are the most common ways to make ophthalmic and parenteral solutions isotonic.

short.q: Explain buffer capacity with the Van Slyke equation. At what pH is buffer capacity maximum?
short.hi: β = 2.303 C Ka[H3O+]/(Ka+[H3O+])²; max at pH = pKa, βmax = 0.576C

kp.t: Depends on total buffer concentration and ratio

a.intro: Buffer capacity (β) is the magnitude of resistance of a buffer to pH change. It is the number of gram equivalents of strong acid or base needed to change the pH of 1 litre of buffer by 1 unit: β = ΔB/ΔpH.
points: Van Slyke equation: β = 2.303 C × Ka[H3O+] / (Ka + [H3O+])², where C = total buffer concentration (acid + salt).
Buffer capacity increases with the total concentration of buffer components.
It is maximum when [H3O+] = Ka, i.e. pH = pKa ([salt] = [acid]); then βmax = 2.303 C/4 = 0.576 C.
β falls as the ratio [salt]/[acid] moves away from 1; a buffer is useful in the range pKa ± 1.
Example: for an acetate buffer with total concentration 0.1 M at pH = pKa (4.76), βmax = 0.0576.
a.diagram: Plot of β (y) vs pH (x): bell-shaped curve with peak at pH = pKa.
a.conclusion: A buffer is most effective near its pKa and at higher total concentration.

short.q: Describe the colorimetric determination of pH. Give the limitations.
short.hi: Indicator का colour pH पर निर्भर; pH = pKIn + log [In-]/[HIn]

kp.t: Indicators are weak acids/bases with different coloured forms
Examples: methyl orange 3.1-4.4, phenolphthalein 8.3-10, bromothymol blue 6.0-7.6
Comparison with standard buffer colours / comparator, pH paper
Limitations: coloured/turbid samples, salt and protein error

a.intro: Colorimetric pH determination uses indicators - weak organic acids or bases whose un-ionised (HIn) and ionised (In-) forms have different colours.
points: Indicator equation: pH = pKIn + log [In-]/[HIn]; colour change is seen over about pKIn ± 1 pH unit.
Common indicators: methyl orange 3.1-4.4 (red to yellow), methyl red 4.4-6.2 (red to yellow), bromothymol blue 6.0-7.6 (yellow to blue), phenolphthalein 8.3-10.0 (colourless to pink).

Method: a suitable indicator is added to the test solution and to a series of standard buffer solutions of known pH; the colour of the test is matched with the standards (in a comparator or colorimeter) to read its pH. Universal indicators and indicator papers give quick approximate values.
Advantages: simple, cheap, no instrument needed.

Limitations: less accurate (about ±0.2 pH); cannot be used for coloured or turbid solutions; errors due to salts (ionic strength), proteins, colloids, oxidising/reducing agents and temperature; the indicator itself may alter the pH of poorly buffered solutions.
a.conclusion: Colorimetric methods are useful for quick checks, but the electrometric (glass electrode) method is preferred for accuracy.

short.q: Discuss buffers in biological systems: blood, lacrimal fluid and urine.
short.hi: Blood 7.4 bicarbonate; tears ~7.4; urine ~6

kp.t: Blood pH 7.4 maintained by bicarbonate, phosphate, proteins, haemoglobin
Lacrimal fluid pH about 7.4; eye tolerates mild deviation

a.intro: Body fluids are buffered so that their pH stays within narrow limits needed for enzymes and cell function.
points: Blood: pH about 7.4 (7.35-7.45). Below this is acidosis, above is alkalosis. Plasma buffers are carbonic acid/bicarbonate (pKa about 6.1, ratio HCO3-:H2CO3 about 20:1 at pH 7.4), phosphate and plasma proteins. In red cells, haemoglobin/oxyhaemoglobin and organic phosphates are the main buffers. Lungs (CO2 removal) and kidneys (HCO3- and H+ handling) adjust the buffer ratio.
Phosphate buffer (H2PO4-/HPO4 2-, pKa about 6.8 at body conditions) is important inside cells and in urine.

Lacrimal fluid (tears): pH about 7.4 with some buffer capacity; ophthalmic solutions should be close to this pH or only weakly buffered so tears can bring them to physiological pH and avoid irritation.

Urine: pH about 6 on average, varying roughly from 4.5 to 7.8 depending on diet and acid-base state; phosphate and ammonia/ammonium buffers carry away acid. Urine pH affects excretion of weak acids and bases (ion trapping).
Pharmaceutical relevance: parenteral and ophthalmic products are formulated with low buffer capacity near physiological pH to reduce pain and irritation.
a.conclusion: Biological buffers keep body pH constant; dosage forms must respect these pH values to be comfortable and safe.

short.q: Explain the factors that influence the pH of buffer solutions.
short.hi: Ionic strength (activity), temperature, dilution, salts का effect

kp.t: Buffer ratio and pKa decide pH
Interaction with drug / container, CO2 absorption

a.intro: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives the pH of a buffer from pKa and the ratio [salt]/[acid], but real buffers are influenced by several factors.
points: Ionic strength: adding neutral salts changes the activity coefficients of the ions; the corrected equation is pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) - 0.5√μ/(1 + √μ) (μ = ionic strength), so salts usually lower the pH of an acidic buffer slightly.
Dilution: on dilution the ratio stays the same, so pH changes only slightly (due to activity changes), but buffer capacity decreases.
Temperature: pKa (and pKw) change with temperature; e.g. the pH of buffers containing basic components (borate, tris) changes notably on heating, which matters during autoclaving.
Buffer ratio and pKa: the main determinants; choose a buffer whose pKa is within ±1 of the required pH.
Other: absorption of atmospheric CO2 (alkaline buffers), alkali leaching from glass containers, and interaction of buffer with the drug or other ingredients.
a.conclusion: Formulators allow for ionic strength, temperature and storage effects when preparing buffers of an exact pH.

long.q: Explain the quantitative approach to the various factors influencing the solubility of drugs. State the Nernst Distribution Law and discuss its pharmaceutical applications and limitations.
long.hi: Solubility factors (temperature, pH, particle size, polymorph) + Nernst K = C1/C2

kp.t: Temperature: van't Hoff / heat of solution
pH and pKa: ionisation increases solubility
Nernst law K = C1/C2 at constant temperature
Limitations: dilute, constant temperature, no association/dissociation
Applications: drug absorption, preservatives in emulsions

a.intro: Solubility is the concentration of solute in a saturated solution at a definite temperature. Several factors influence it in a measurable (quantitative) way; the distribution of a solute between two immiscible phases is described by the Nernst distribution law.
points: Temperature: ln(X2) varies with 1/T (van't Hoff equation); solubility rises with temperature for endothermic (positive heat of solution) solutes and falls for exothermic ones.

pH: for a weak acid, total solubility S = S0 (1 + 10^(pH - pKa)); for a weak base, S = S0 (1 + 10^(pKa - pH)), where S0 is solubility of the un-ionised form. The pH below which a weak acid precipitates (pHp) is pHp = pKa + log[(S - S0)/S0].
Particle size: very fine particles are more soluble: log(S/S0) = 2γV/(2.303 R T r) (Ostwald-Freundlich equation), where r = particle radius.
Molecular structure, polymorphism and crystal form: metastable polymorphs and amorphous forms have lower lattice energy and higher solubility.

Co-solvents (ethanol, PEG, propylene glycol) reduce polarity of water: log S of mixture changes roughly linearly with fraction of co-solvent; surfactants above CMC solubilise drugs in micelles; complexing agents form soluble complexes; common ion effect lowers solubility (Ksp).
Nernst distribution law: at constant temperature, a solute distributes between two immiscible solvents so that K = C1/C2 is constant (partition or distribution coefficient).
Modifications: for association in one phase K = C1^(1/n)/C2; for dissociation only the un-ionised fraction is used.
Limitations: valid only at constant temperature, in dilute solutions, with mutually immiscible solvents, when solute is in the same molecular form in both phases and does not react with the solvent.

Applications: solvent extraction of drugs (several small extractions are more efficient), partition chromatography, prediction of absorption and distribution (log P), preservative action in emulsions, study of association and complexation.
a.diagram: Graph: solubility of a weak acid vs pH showing a flat region (S0) at low pH rising sharply above pKa. Also a separating funnel with organic layer C1 and aqueous layer C2.
a.conclusion: Quantitative relations let the formulator predict and improve solubility, and the distribution law links solubility to extraction and drug absorption.

long.q: Discuss the mechanisms of solute-solvent interactions. Explain ideal solubility parameters and the role of solvation and association in solubility.
long.hi: Polar/non-polar/semi-polar solvents, ideal solubility equation, Hildebrand δ

kp.t: Polar solvents: dielectric constant, H-bonds, ion-dipole
Ideal solubility equation (heat of fusion, melting point)

a.intro: A solute dissolves when solute-solvent attractions can overcome solute-solute (crystal lattice) and solvent-solvent attractions. The type of solvent decides which forces operate.
points: Polar solvents (water, alcohols, glycerin) dissolve ionic and polar solutes because of (a) high dielectric constant, which reduces attraction between oppositely charged ions; (b) breaking covalent bonds of strong electrolytes by acid-base reactions; (c) solvation through ion-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding (e.g. phenols, alcohols, amines dissolve in water).

Non-polar solvents (hexane, benzene, CCl4, oils) have low dielectric constant and cannot form H-bonds; they dissolve non-polar solutes through weak London (induced dipole-induced dipole) forces, e.g. fixed oils, alkaloidal bases.

Semi-polar solvents (ketones, alcohols) induce a dipole in non-polar molecules and act as intermediates that increase miscibility of polar and non-polar liquids (e.g. acetone increases solubility of ether in water).
Ideal solubility: log X2 = -(ΔHf/2.303 R)(T0 - T)/(T T0); depends only on heat of fusion and melting point of the solute, not on the solvent.
Regular solutions: log X2 = log X2(ideal) - V2 Φ1² (δ1 - δ2)²/(2.303 R T), where δ is the Hildebrand solubility parameter.
Solubility parameter δ = [(ΔHv - RT)/V]^1/2 = square root of cohesive energy density; maximum solubility when δ of solute ≈ δ of solvent.
Solvation: binding of solvent molecules to solute (hydration in water) releases energy that helps break the crystal lattice; solvates/hydrates often have different solubility from anhydrous forms.
Association: solute molecules join together (e.g. carboxylic acid dimers in non-polar solvents, surfactant micelles in water), changing apparent molecular weight, solubility and partition behaviour.
a.diagram: Table-like sketch: three columns (polar, semi-polar, non-polar solvents) with dielectric constant decreasing from left to right and examples of solutes dissolved in each.
a.conclusion: Solubility is predicted by comparing polarity, dielectric constant and solubility parameters of solute and solvent, corrected for solvation and association.

long.q: Explain the solubility of gases in liquids with Henry's law and the factors affecting it. Discuss diffusion principles in biological systems.
long.hi: Henry's law + Fick's law, passive diffusion across membranes

a.intro: Solubility of a gas in a liquid is the concentration of dissolved gas in equilibrium with the gas above the liquid at given temperature and pressure. It is important for carbonated solutions, aerosols, oxygen in blood and oxidation of drugs.
points: Henry's law: C2 = σ p2; concentration of dissolved gas is proportional to its partial pressure at constant temperature (σ = solubility coefficient).
Effect of pressure: higher pressure dissolves more gas; on release of pressure gas escapes (e.g. opening a soda bottle, effervescent preparations).
Effect of temperature: gas solubility decreases as temperature increases; dissolved gases are expelled by boiling water.
Salting out: electrolytes (and some non-electrolytes like sucrose) reduce gas solubility because ions attract water molecules.
Chemical reaction: gases that react with the solvent (HCl, NH3, CO2) show much greater solubility and do not obey Henry's law.
Diffusion: spontaneous movement of molecules from higher to lower concentration due to random motion.
Fick's first law: J = -D (dC/dx), flux is proportional to concentration gradient; D is the diffusion coefficient (depends on molecular size, viscosity, temperature).

Biological systems: most drugs cross GI epithelium, skin, blood-brain barrier and placenta by passive diffusion; rate dQ/dt = D A K (C1 - C2)/h, where K = partition coefficient, A = area, h = membrane thickness.
Lipid-soluble, un-ionised and small molecules diffuse fastest; diffusion also controls release from transdermal patches and matrix tablets.
a.diagram: Draw a membrane of thickness h between a donor compartment (high concentration C1) and receiver compartment (low C2) with an arrow showing direction of diffusion.
a.conclusion: Henry's law governs dissolved gases in pharmaceutical liquids, while Fick's law explains how drugs move through biological membranes.

long.q: Explain the solubility of liquids in liquids. Discuss vapour pressure-composition and boiling point-composition diagrams of ideal and non-ideal binary solutions.
long.hi: Binary solutions: ideal straight line, real में maximum/minimum, azeotrope

kp.t: Ideal binary solution follows Raoult's law
Vapour richer in more volatile component
Boiling point diagram: liquid and vapour curves

a.intro: Liquid pairs may be completely miscible (ethanol-water), partially miscible (phenol-water) or immiscible (oil-water). Completely miscible pairs form binary solutions whose vapour pressure and boiling point depend on composition.
points: Ideal binary solutions obey Raoult's law: pA = pA° XA and pB = pB° XB; total vapour pressure is a straight line joining pB° and pA° on a VP-mole fraction plot.
The vapour above a solution is richer in the more volatile component (Dalton's law: yA = pA/P); this is why distillation can separate liquids.

Boiling point-composition diagram of an ideal system: lower liquid (bubble point) curve and upper vapour (dew point) curve meeting at the boiling points of the pure liquids; the lens-shaped area between them is the two-phase region.

Positive deviation (weaker A-B forces): VP curve lies above the ideal line and may show a maximum; the boiling point curve then shows a minimum (minimum-boiling azeotrope, e.g. ethanol-water at about 95.6% ethanol).
Negative deviation (stronger A-B forces, H-bonding): VP curve lies below the ideal line and may show a minimum; boiling point curve shows a maximum (maximum-boiling azeotrope, e.g. HCl-water).
At the azeotropic composition the liquid and vapour have the same composition, so fractional distillation cannot separate beyond the azeotrope.
Very large positive deviation leads to partial miscibility and two liquid layers.
Pharmaceutical importance: purification of solvents by fractional distillation, choice of solvent mixtures, recovery of alcohol, and propellant blends in aerosols.
a.diagram: Draw (1) VP vs mole fraction for ideal (straight lines), positive (curve with maximum) and negative (curve with minimum) systems; (2) boiling point vs composition with liquid and vapour curves; mark the azeotrope point where they touch.
a.conclusion: Phase diagrams of binary liquids explain distillation, azeotropes and the behaviour of mixed solvents used in pharmacy.

long.q: Discuss the states of matter and the changes in the state of matter. Explain latent heats, vapour pressure and the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
long.hi: Solid, liquid, gas; latent heat; Clausius-Clapeyron

kp.t: Three states: solid, liquid, gas (intermolecular forces)
Changes: melting, freezing, vaporization, condensation, sublimation
Latent heat of fusion and vaporization
Vapour pressure: equilibrium, increases with temperature
Boiling point: VP equals external pressure

a.intro: Matter exists in three main states: solid, liquid and gas, depending on the balance between intermolecular attractive forces and the kinetic (thermal) energy of the molecules. Intermediate states (liquid crystals, supercritical fluids) also exist.
points: Gases: molecules far apart, weak attractions, no fixed shape or volume, compressible; behaviour described by PV = nRT.
Liquids: molecules close together with moderate attraction; fixed volume but no fixed shape; show vapour pressure, surface tension and viscosity.
Solids: strong attractions, fixed shape and volume; crystalline or amorphous.

Changes of state: melting (fusion), freezing, vaporization (evaporation/boiling), condensation, sublimation and deposition. They occur at constant temperature with absorption or release of latent heat.

Latent heat of fusion: heat absorbed when unit mass of solid melts at its melting point (ice ≈ 80 cal/g). Latent heat of vaporization: heat absorbed when unit mass of liquid vaporises at its boiling point (water ≈ 540 cal/g at 100°C).
Vapour pressure: pressure of vapour in equilibrium with the liquid in a closed container at a given temperature; depends on nature of liquid and temperature, not on amount of liquid.

Clausius-Clapeyron equation: log(p2/p1) = ΔHv (T2 - T1)/(2.303 R T1 T2); a plot of log p vs 1/T is a straight line with slope -ΔHv/2.303R, used to calculate heat of vaporization or VP at another temperature.
Boiling point: temperature at which vapour pressure equals the external pressure; lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point (basis of vacuum distillation and evaporation).
Trouton's rule: ΔHv/Tb ≈ 21 cal/mol·K (about 88 J/mol·K) for many non-associated liquids.
Pharmaceutical importance: drying, evaporation, distillation, freeze drying, aerosol propellants and storage of volatile drugs depend on these properties.
a.diagram: Graph of log p (y) vs 1/T (x) showing a straight line with negative slope (Clausius-Clapeyron plot); and a heating curve (temperature vs heat added) with flat steps at melting and boiling.
a.conclusion: Understanding state changes and their energy requirements is essential for unit operations and for stability of drugs.

long.q: What are aerosols? Explain the principle and components of metered dose inhalers and dry powder inhalers. Add a note on the properties of gases relevant to aerosols.
long.hi: Aerosol: propellant + valve + actuator; MDI, DPI

kp.t: Aerosol: pressurised dosage form, fine dispersion in gas
Propellant: liquefied gas (HFA 134a, HFA 227) or compressed gas
Particle size 1-5 µm for lung deposition
Gas laws: PV = nRT, Dalton's law of partial pressures

a.intro: Aerosols are pressurised dosage forms that release the drug as a fine dispersion of solid or liquid particles in a gas. Inhalation aerosols deliver drugs directly to the lungs (e.g. salbutamol, beclomethasone).
points: Principle: a liquefied propellant in a sealed container exerts its vapour pressure; on pressing the valve, the contents are expelled, the propellant flashes (evaporates) instantly and leaves fine drug particles/droplets.

Gas laws behind aerosols: Boyle's, Charles' and the ideal gas law PV = nRT; the pressure inside a liquefied gas aerosol stays constant (equal to propellant vapour pressure) until the liquid is used up. Dalton's law: total pressure = sum of partial pressures; Raoult's law gives the vapour pressure of propellant blends.
MDI components - Container: aluminium (most common), stainless steel, glass or tin plate; must resist pressure and corrosion.
Propellant: chlorofluorocarbons (CFC 11, 12, 114) earlier; now ozone-friendly hydrofluoroalkanes HFA-134a and HFA-227; hydrocarbons and compressed gases (N2, CO2, N2O) for topical aerosols.
Metering valve: delivers an accurate fixed volume (dose) each actuation; has a metering chamber, stem, spring and gaskets.
Actuator: mouthpiece with an orifice that breaks the spray into fine particles and directs it into the mouth; spacers improve deposition and reduce co-ordination problems.
Formulation: drug dissolved (solution MDI, with co-solvent ethanol) or suspended (suspension MDI, with surfactants such as oleic acid, lecithin).

Dry powder inhalers: propellant-free; micronised drug (1-5 µm) blended with coarse lactose carrier; breath-actuated (patient's inspiration disperses powder); unit dose (capsule) or multi-dose reservoir devices.
Particle size: 1-5 µm reach the lower airways; larger particles deposit in the throat; very small (<0.5 µm) are exhaled.

Advantages: rapid local action, low dose, fewer systemic side effects, sterile and tamper-proof container; disadvantages: need for patient co-ordination (MDI), cost, propellant toxicity/environment issues.
a.diagram: Draw a pressurised MDI: canister containing drug + liquefied propellant (liquid phase below, vapour phase above), dip tube/metering valve, stem pressed into the actuator, and spray plume from the mouthpiece.
a.conclusion: Aerosols use the vapour pressure of liquefied gases to deliver precise doses of drugs directly to the lungs.

long.q: Explain dielectric constant and dipole moment. Describe their determination and pharmaceutical applications.
long.hi: ε = C/C0; μ = q × d (Debye); Debye equation

kp.t: Applications: molecular structure (CO2 zero, water bent)

a.intro: Dielectric constant and dipole moment describe the electrical (polar) properties of molecules. They help explain solubility, solvent action and molecular structure.
points: Dielectric constant (ε): ratio of capacitance of a condenser filled with the substance (C) to its capacitance with vacuum (C0): ε = C/C0. It shows the ability of a substance to reduce the electric force between charges; water ≈ 78.5, ethanol ≈ 24, chloroform ≈ 4.8, hexane ≈ 1.9.

Determination of ε: the substance is placed between the plates of a condenser in a dielectric constant meter (capacitance bridge or resonance/heterodyne method) and capacitance is compared with that of air/vacuum.
Induced polarization: a non-polar molecule placed in an electric field gets a temporary dipole; molar polarization Pi = [(ε - 1)/(ε + 2)] × (M/ρ) (Clausius-Mossotti equation).
Dipole moment (μ): product of the magnitude of separated charge and the distance between them: μ = q × d; unit Debye (1 D = 10^-18 esu·cm = 3.336 × 10^-30 C·m). Water ≈ 1.84 D.
Debye equation: P = (4/3)πN (α0 + μ²/3kT). Total polarization is measured at several temperatures; a plot of P vs 1/T is linear, slope gives μ and intercept gives polarizability α0.

Applications in structure: CO2 and CCl4 have zero dipole moment (symmetrical, linear/tetrahedral), water has a dipole (bent molecule); cis isomers have larger μ than trans; ortho, meta and para disubstituted benzenes can be distinguished.

Pharmaceutical applications: choice of solvents and co-solvent blends of a required dielectric constant to dissolve drugs (drugs dissolve best in solvents of similar ε); explains solubility of electrolytes in water; relates polarity to drug-receptor binding, permeability and partition; used to predict stability of drugs in different solvents.
a.diagram: Draw a parallel-plate condenser with and without a dielectric between the plates (showing dipoles aligning with the field), and a graph of molar polarization (y) vs 1/T (x) with straight line.
a.conclusion: Dielectric constant and dipole moment quantify polarity, which governs solubility and molecular interactions of drugs.

long.q: Write notes on liquid crystals, glassy state and liquid complexes. Give their pharmaceutical significance.
long.hi: Liquid crystal: mesophase - smectic, nematic, cholesteric; thermotropic/lyotropic

kp.t: Liquid crystal: mesophase between solid and liquid

a.intro: Some substances show states intermediate between crystalline solids and isotropic liquids (liquid crystals) or between liquid and solid (glassy, amorphous state). These states affect stability and drug delivery.
points: Liquid crystals (mesophases): flow like liquids but keep some order like crystals; molecules are usually rod-like and show anisotropy and birefringence (double refraction).

Thermotropic liquid crystals form on heating a solid (e.g. cholesteryl benzoate); lyotropic liquid crystals form when a substance (usually a surfactant or soap) is mixed with a solvent such as water at suitable concentration.
Smectic (soap-like): molecules arranged in layers, mobile in two directions (within the layer); viscous.
Nematic (thread-like): molecules parallel but not in layers, mobile in three directions; less viscous.
Cholesteric: nematic layers with a twist from layer to layer (chiral); change colour with temperature (used in thermometers).

Pharmaceutical significance: lyotropic liquid crystalline phases of surfactants stabilise emulsions and creams; used for controlled release (cubic and hexagonal phases of glyceryl monooleate), solubilisation, cosmetics and transdermal systems; biological membranes have liquid crystalline character.

Glassy state: an amorphous solid formed by rapid cooling or drying; below glass transition temperature (Tg) it is hard and brittle with very low molecular mobility; above Tg it becomes rubbery. Freeze-dried products and amorphous solid dispersions are glasses; storage below Tg improves stability, and water (plasticizer) lowers Tg.

Liquid complexes: some drugs form liquid (low melting) complexes or ionic liquids with other molecules or counter-ions, which can increase solubility and permeation; eutectic-like liquid mixtures (e.g. lidocaine-prilocaine) are used topically.
a.diagram: Draw molecular arrangement sketches: crystal (ordered lattice), smectic (rods in layers), nematic (rods parallel, no layers), isotropic liquid (random rods).
a.conclusion: Mesophases and glasses are intermediate states that formulators use to control solubility, stability and drug release.

long.q: Define dissociation constant. Describe the methods for determination of pKa of drugs and discuss its applications.
long.hi: pKa: potentiometric titration, spectrophotometric, solubility method

kp.t: Potentiometric titration: pH at half neutralization = pKa
Applications: solubility, salt and buffer selection

a.intro: Most drugs are weak acids or weak bases. The dissociation constant (Ka) measures how strongly they ionise: for HA + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + A-, Ka = [H3O+][A-]/[HA] and pKa = -log Ka.
points: For bases, BH+ ⇌ B + H+ and pKa refers to the conjugate acid; pKa + pKb = pKw (14 at 25°C).
