From Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); when [A-] = [HA], pH = pKa (drug is 50% ionised).

Potentiometric titration: the drug solution is titrated with standard NaOH (or HCl) and pH is measured with a glass electrode after each addition; the pH at the half-equivalence point equals pKa. Simple and accurate for drugs soluble enough in water (co-solvent extrapolation for poorly soluble ones).

Spectrophotometric method: used when ionised and un-ionised forms have different UV spectra; absorbance at a fixed wavelength is measured in buffers of different pH; pKa = pH + log[(A_I - A)/(A - A_M)] (for an acid, A_I = absorbance of ionised form, A_M = molecular form). Useful for sparingly soluble drugs.
Solubility method: solubility is measured at different pH; for a weak acid S = S0[1 + 10^(pH - pKa)]; pKa is calculated from the pH-solubility profile.
Conductivity method: degree of dissociation α = Λ/Λ0, then Ka = α²C/(1 - α) (Ostwald dilution law).

Applications: predicting the fraction ionised at physiological pH; absorption by the pH-partition hypothesis (un-ionised form crosses membranes - weak acids like aspirin absorbed more in stomach); solubility and dissolution; choice of salt forms and buffers; stability; renal excretion and ion trapping.
a.diagram: Titration curve: pH (y) vs volume of NaOH (x) showing a buffer region with the point at half-neutralisation marked 'pH = pKa' and a steep rise at the equivalence point.
a.conclusion: pKa is one of the most important physicochemical parameters for predicting solubility, absorption and formulation of drugs.

long.q: Define surface and interfacial tension. Describe in detail the principle and working of the capillary rise method for the measurement of surface tension.
long.hi: Capillary rise: γ = ½ r h ρ g

kp.t: Surface tension: force per unit length (dyne/cm)
Interfacial tension: between two immiscible liquids
Cause: unbalanced inward pull on surface molecules
Liquid rises in capillary due to adhesion
γ = ½ r h ρ g (θ = 0)
Limitations: only liquids that wet glass, not interfacial

a.intro: Surface tension (γ) is the force per unit length acting parallel to the surface of a liquid, at right angles to any line drawn on it. It arises because molecules at the surface experience a net inward pull from the bulk. Unit: dyne/cm (mN/m); water ≈ 72.8 dyne/cm at 20°C. Interfacial tension is the force per unit length at the interface between two immiscible liquids (e.g. oil and water); it is usually lower than the higher of the two surface tensions.
points: Principle: when a capillary tube is dipped in a liquid that wets glass, adhesive forces pull the liquid up; it rises until the upward force due to surface tension is balanced by the downward weight of the liquid column.
Upward force: acts along the inner circumference 2πr: F(up) = 2πr γ cosθ, θ = contact angle (about 0° for water on clean glass, so cosθ = 1).
Downward force: weight of liquid column = mass × g = πr²h ρ g (neglecting the meniscus).
At equilibrium: 2πr γ cosθ = πr²h ρ g, so γ = r h ρ g / (2 cosθ); for θ = 0, γ = ½ r h ρ g.

Apparatus: clean, uniform-bore capillary tube held vertically in the liquid in a beaker, with a travelling microscope to read the height of the meniscus above the liquid level; temperature controlled.
Procedure: measure radius r of the capillary (e.g. with the travelling microscope or by mercury thread weighing), dip it in the liquid, read h, know density ρ, and calculate γ.
Relative method: γ1/γ2 = h1ρ1/(h2ρ2) using water as reference.
Advantages: simple, accurate, inexpensive; one of the most accurate methods.
Limitations: needs liquids that wet glass completely; cannot measure interfacial tension; tube must be very clean and of uniform bore; small correction for the meniscus volume is needed.
a.diagram: Draw a beaker of liquid with a capillary tube dipped vertically; liquid column risen to height h with a concave meniscus; arrows showing surface tension γ pulling upward along the walls at contact angle θ and weight acting downward; radius r marked.
a.conclusion: The capillary rise method gives accurate surface tension from simple measurements of height, radius and density.

long.q: Explain the methods of measuring surface and interfacial tension other than capillary rise: drop count/drop weight method, du Noüy ring method and Wilhelmy plate method.
long.hi: Stalagmometer, du Noüy tensiometer, Wilhelmy plate

kp.t: Weight of drop = 2πrγ (Tate's law), Harkins-Brown correction
du Noüy ring: force to detach platinum ring
Interfacial tension measured by ring/drop methods

a.intro: Besides capillary rise, surface tension (liquid-air) and interfacial tension (liquid-liquid) are measured by drop methods, the du Noüy ring tensiometer and the Wilhelmy plate.
points: Drop weight and drop count method (stalagmometer): a liquid flows slowly from a capillary tip; a drop falls when its weight exceeds the force of surface tension holding it, W = mg = 2πr γ (Tate's law, r = tip radius), with Harkins-Brown correction factor because only part of the drop falls.
Drop count: the number of drops (n) formed from a fixed volume is counted for the test liquid and for water: γ1/γ2 = (n2 ρ1)/(n1 ρ2). Drop weight: γ1/γ2 = W1/W2.
Interfacial tension can be measured by forming drops of one liquid under the surface of the other.

du Noüy ring method: a platinum-iridium ring is placed in the liquid surface and the force needed to detach it is measured with a torsion balance (tensiometer). γ = (dial reading / 2 × circumference) × β = F/(4πR) × β, where R = ring radius and β = correction factor.
For interfacial tension the ring is placed at the interface of the two liquids and pulled through from the lower to the upper phase.

Wilhelmy plate method: a thin platinum or glass plate is dipped vertically in the liquid; the downward pull on the plate (measured by a balance) equals γ × perimeter (cosθ, θ ≈ 0): γ = F / [2(l + t)], where l = length and t = thickness of plate.
Precautions: ring and plate are cleaned by flaming; temperature controlled; ring kept horizontal.

Comparison: drop methods are simple and cheap; du Noüy ring is quick and widely used for both surface and interfacial tension; Wilhelmy plate needs no correction factor and can follow changes with time.
a.diagram: Draw (1) stalagmometer: glass tube with bulb, upper and lower marks, capillary tip with a drop forming; (2) du Noüy tensiometer: torsion wire, dial, lever arm with platinum ring touching the liquid surface in a dish; (3) Wilhelmy plate hanging from a balance into a liquid.
a.conclusion: Choice of method depends on the liquid, accuracy needed and whether surface or interfacial tension is to be measured.

long.q: Explain adsorption at the solid interface. Discuss Freundlich and Langmuir adsorption isotherms, factors affecting adsorption and its pharmaceutical applications.
long.hi: Freundlich x/m = kc^(1/n); Langmuir monolayer; activated charcoal

kp.t: Adsorption: surface accumulation on solid adsorbent
Physical (van der Waals) vs chemical adsorption
Factors: temperature, surface area, pH, nature

a.intro: Adsorption at a solid interface is the accumulation of molecules of a gas or solute (adsorbate) on the surface of a solid (adsorbent). It is a surface phenomenon, unlike absorption, which involves the bulk.
points: Physical adsorption: due to weak van der Waals forces, low heat of adsorption, reversible, multilayer, decreases with rise in temperature, non-specific.
Chemical adsorption (chemisorption): due to chemical bonds, high heat of adsorption, irreversible, monolayer, specific, may increase with temperature initially.
Freundlich isotherm (empirical): x/m = k c^(1/n) (or k p^(1/n)); log(x/m) = log k + (1/n) log c gives a straight line; fails at high concentration.

Langmuir isotherm: assumes a monolayer, uniform surface sites and no interaction between adsorbed molecules: x/m = y = ab c/(1 + b c); linear form c/y = 1/(ab) + c/a, where a = monolayer capacity, b = constant related to affinity.
BET equation (Brunauer, Emmett, Teller): extends Langmuir to multilayer adsorption; used to measure specific surface area of powders by nitrogen adsorption.

Factors: nature and surface area of adsorbent (finely divided, porous solids adsorb more), nature of adsorbate (less soluble solutes adsorb more), temperature (physical adsorption decreases with heat), pH (affects ionisation), concentration or pressure, competing solutes.

Applications: activated charcoal as an antidote in drug overdose and poisoning; kaolin and attapulgite as antidiarrhoeal adsorbents; decolourisation and purification of solutions; chromatography (adsorption columns, TLC); gas masks; surface area measurement of powders; adsorption of preservatives and drugs on containers, filters and excipients (e.g. reduced availability with magnesium trisilicate).
a.diagram: Plot x/m (y) vs c or p (x): Freundlich curve rising and flattening; Langmuir curve reaching a plateau (monolayer saturation). Also log(x/m) vs log c straight line for Freundlich.
a.conclusion: Adsorption on solids is widely used in therapy, purification and analysis, and can also reduce drug availability.

long.q: What are surface active agents? Discuss their properties, micelle formation and CMC, and explain solubilisation and detergency.
long.hi: Surfactant: amphiphile; micelle; solubilisation; detergency

kp.t: Detergency: removal of dirt (wetting, emulsifying, suspending)

a.intro: Surface active agents (surfactants) are amphiphilic molecules having a hydrophilic (polar) head and a lipophilic (non-polar hydrocarbon) tail. They adsorb at interfaces and lower surface and interfacial tension.
points: Classification: anionic (sodium lauryl sulphate, soaps), cationic (benzalkonium chloride, cetrimide), non-ionic (Spans, Tweens, macrogol ethers), ampholytic (lecithin).
Properties: positive adsorption at interfaces, lowering of surface/interfacial tension, wetting, emulsifying, foaming, solubilising and detergent actions; cationics are also antimicrobial.

Micelle formation: at low concentration surfactant molecules collect at the surface; when the surface is saturated, further molecules aggregate in the bulk into micelles (spherical in dilute solution) with tails inside and heads facing water. Reverse micelles form in non-polar solvents.

CMC: concentration at which micelles start to form; detected by breaks in plots of surface tension, conductivity, osmotic pressure or light scattering vs concentration. CMC decreases with increase in hydrocarbon chain length and on adding electrolytes (for ionic surfactants).
Krafft point: temperature above which solubility of ionic surfactant rises sharply (micelles form); cloud point: temperature at which non-ionic surfactant solution becomes turbid on heating.

Solubilisation: spontaneous dissolution of poorly water-soluble substances in surfactant micelles to form a thermodynamically stable, clear solution; begins above CMC. Non-polar solutes go into the hydrocarbon core, semi-polar ones into the palisade layer, polar ones on the micelle surface. Examples: vitamins A, D, E and K, steroids, essential oils solubilised by polysorbates; cresol with soap (Lysol).

Detergency: removal of grease and dirt from a surface; involves wetting of the surface, penetration and removal of dirt by emulsification or solubilisation, suspension of particles and prevention of redeposition, and foaming. Surfactants with HLB 13-15 are good detergents.
Pharmaceutical uses: emulsifiers, wetting agents in suspensions, solubilisers, detergents and antiseptics, absorption enhancers.
a.diagram: Draw a spherical micelle in water: circles (heads) on the outside, tails pointing to the centre; a solubilised drug molecule in the core. Also a graph of surface tension vs log concentration falling and then becoming flat at the CMC.
a.conclusion: Surfactants, through micelle formation, make solubilisation and detergency possible and are among the most used excipients.

long.q: Discuss protein binding of drugs: mechanism, factors affecting it, and its significance in drug action (complexation and drug action).
long.hi: Free drug ही active; albumin binding; displacement interactions

kp.t: Reversible binding mainly to albumin and α1-acid glycoprotein
Forces: ionic, hydrogen bond, hydrophobic, van der Waals
Factors: drug properties, protein concentration, disease
Effect on distribution and volume of distribution

a.intro: Many drugs bind reversibly to plasma proteins and tissue components, forming drug-protein complexes. Bound drug is inactive, cannot cross membranes and acts as a reservoir; only the free (unbound) drug produces effect and is metabolised and excreted.
points: Binding proteins: albumin (most abundant; binds acidic drugs like warfarin, salicylates, phenylbutazone, sulfonamides), α1-acid glycoprotein (basic drugs like propranolol, lidocaine), lipoproteins (lipophilic drugs) and globulins.

Forces involved: ionic (electrostatic) bonds, hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and van der Waals forces; the binding is usually reversible and obeys the law of mass action: Drug + Protein ⇌ Drug-Protein complex.
Drug-related factors: physicochemical properties (lipophilicity, ionisation), drug concentration (binding sites can be saturated), affinity for the protein.
Protein-related factors: protein concentration (hypoalbuminaemia in liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, burns, malnutrition, old age increases free drug), number of binding sites.
Other factors: competing drugs and endogenous substances (bilirubin, fatty acids), pH, temperature, disease states (uraemia), pregnancy and neonatal age.
Significance - activity: only unbound drug reaches the receptor; highly bound drugs have small free fraction.

Distribution: plasma protein binding restricts distribution to tissues (smaller volume of distribution), while tissue binding increases it; bound drug cannot cross the blood-brain barrier or placenta.
Elimination: bound drug is not filtered by the glomerulus and is protected from metabolism, so highly bound drugs often have longer half-life and duration (acts as depot).
Displacement interactions: phenylbutazone or aspirin displaces warfarin → bleeding; sulfonamides displace tolbutamide → hypoglycaemia; sulfonamides displace bilirubin in neonates → kernicterus.
Diagnostic and therapeutic use: binding data (free fraction) guide dosing in hypoalbuminaemia and therapeutic drug monitoring.
a.diagram: Draw blood plasma with drug molecules: some attached to albumin (bound, large circle) and some free; arrow showing only free drug crossing the capillary wall to the receptor/tissue; equilibrium arrows between bound and free.
a.conclusion: Protein binding controls the free drug concentration and therefore the intensity, distribution and duration of drug action.

long.q: Describe the methods of analysis of complexes: method of continuous variation (Job's method), pH titration method, distribution method and spectroscopic methods.
long.hi: Job's plot maximum = stoichiometry; pH titration shift; distribution method

kp.t: Job's method: vary mole fraction, total concentration constant
Plot of property difference vs mole fraction; maximum gives ratio
pH titration (Bjerrum): curve shifts on complexation
Distribution method: partition between two phases changes
Example: iodine-KI distribution between water and CCl4
Spectroscopy: UV shift, NMR, IR; Benesi-Hildebrand

a.intro: Complexes are analysed to find their stoichiometry (ratio of components) and stability constant. Common methods are continuous variation, pH titration, distribution, solubility and spectroscopic methods.
points: Method of continuous variation (Job's method): equimolar solutions of metal (or substrate) and ligand are mixed in different proportions so that the total molar concentration stays constant while the mole fraction changes from 0 to 1.

An additive physical property (absorbance, dielectric constant, refractive index) is measured; the difference (Δ) between the observed value and the value expected for no complexation is plotted against mole fraction.
The maximum (or minimum) of the plot appears at the mole fraction corresponding to the complex ratio: 0.5 for 1:1, 0.33 or 0.67 for 1:2/2:1. Works best when only one complex forms.

pH titration method (Bjerrum): used when complexation releases or takes up protons (e.g. glycine with Cu2+). The ligand is titrated with base with and without metal ion; the curve with metal is shifted to lower pH because protons are released. From the shift, the average number of ligands bound (n̄) and stepwise stability constants are calculated.

Distribution method: the partition of a substance between two immiscible solvents changes when it forms a complex in one phase. Example: iodine distributes between water and CCl4; adding KI to the water forms KI3, and from the change in distribution the amount complexed and K are found. Also used for caffeine-benzoic acid/benzocaine complexes.
Solubility method (Higuchi-Connors): changes in solubility of the drug with increasing ligand concentration give phase solubility diagrams (AL, AP, AN, BS, BI).

Spectroscopic methods: UV-visible spectra change (shift in λmax or absorbance) on complex formation; Benesi-Hildebrand equation gives K for 1:1 charge-transfer complexes; NMR and IR shifts show the site of interaction; fluorescence and conductance also used.
Other methods: conductometry, polarography, potentiometry with ion-selective electrodes, calorimetry.
a.diagram: Job's plot: Δ absorbance (y) vs mole fraction of ligand from 0 to 1 (x), showing two straight lines meeting in a peak at 0.5 (1:1 complex). Also pH titration curves of ligand alone and ligand + metal (shifted to lower pH).
a.conclusion: Each method has its own conditions; together they give the composition and stability of drug complexes.

long.q: Explain the crystalline structures of complexes and the thermodynamic treatment of stability constants.
long.hi: ΔG° = -2.303RT log K; ΔG = ΔH - TΔS; coordination geometry

kp.t: Stepwise and overall stability constants (K1, K2, β)
van't Hoff: log K vs 1/T slope -ΔH/2.303R
X-ray diffraction reveals structure; inclusion host lattices

a.intro: The stability of a complex is expressed by its stability (formation) constant, which can be related to free energy, enthalpy and entropy changes. The three-dimensional structure of complexes is studied in the crystalline state, mainly by X-ray diffraction.
points: Stepwise formation: M + A ⇌ MA (K1 = [MA]/[M][A]); MA + A ⇌ MA2 (K2 = [MA2]/[MA][A]); overall stability constant βn = K1 × K2 × ... × Kn. Usually K1 > K2 > K3.
Free energy: ΔG° = -RT ln K = -2.303 RT log K; a large K means a large negative ΔG° (spontaneous, stable complex).

ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°; ΔH° is obtained from the temperature dependence of K (van't Hoff equation): log K = -ΔH°/(2.303 R T) + ΔS°/(2.303 R); a plot of log K vs 1/T has slope -ΔH°/2.303R. ΔS° is then calculated.

Negative ΔH indicates bond formation (exothermic, e.g. metal-ligand coordinate bonds, hydrogen bonds); positive ΔS often reflects release of solvent molecules (hydrophobic interactions, as in cyclodextrin and protein binding).
Chelate effect: chelates are more stable than comparable complexes with monodentate ligands mainly because of a favourable entropy change (one multidentate ligand displaces several water molecules).

Crystalline structures of metal complexes: coordination number 2 - linear (e.g. [Ag(NH3)2]+); 4 - tetrahedral or square planar (e.g. [Cu(NH3)4]2+ square planar); 6 - octahedral (e.g. [Co(NH3)6]3+, EDTA complexes).

Crystalline inclusion compounds: urea forms a hexagonal channel lattice around straight-chain molecules; deoxycholic acid forms choleic acid channels; hydroquinone forms cage (clathrate) lattices; clays form layer lattices. The host exists in this form only with the guest present.
Organic molecular complexes (e.g. quinhydrone) form crystals with alternating donor and acceptor molecules stacked face to face (charge-transfer).
a.diagram: Draw an octahedral complex (metal at centre, 6 ligands at corners) and a square planar complex; and a van't Hoff plot of log K vs 1/T (straight line).
a.conclusion: Thermodynamic parameters explain why complexes form and how temperature affects their stability, while crystal structures show their geometry.

long.q: Describe the methods for determination of protein binding of drugs: equilibrium dialysis, ultrafiltration, dynamic dialysis and gel filtration.
long.hi: Equilibrium dialysis: semipermeable membrane के दोनों तरफ free drug बराबर

kp.t: Equilibrium dialysis: semipermeable membrane, free drug equal both sides
Ultrafiltration: pressure/centrifuge, filtrate has free drug
Dynamic dialysis: rate of loss from bag

a.intro: In protein binding studies the free (unbound) drug concentration must be separated and measured in the presence of protein; bound drug = total drug - free drug. Commonly used methods are dialysis, ultrafiltration and gel filtration.
points: Equilibrium dialysis: a semipermeable membrane (e.g. cellophane) separates a protein solution (with drug) from a buffer compartment. Small drug molecules pass, protein does not. At equilibrium (several hours, constant temperature with shaking) free drug concentration is equal on both sides; the drug in the buffer side gives free drug, and bound = total in protein side - free.
Advantages of equilibrium dialysis: simple, considered the reference method. Disadvantages: long time, drug adsorption to membrane, volume shifts and Donnan effect.

Ultrafiltration: the protein-drug solution is forced through a membrane by pressure or centrifugation; the ultrafiltrate contains only free drug. Fast and suitable for clinical samples, but binding to membrane and changes in equilibrium during filtration can cause error.

Dynamic dialysis: the protein-drug solution is placed in a dialysis bag in a large volume of buffer; the rate of loss of drug from the bag is measured; since rate is proportional to free drug concentration, the free concentration is calculated at each time.

Gel filtration (molecular filtration): a Sephadex column separates the large protein-drug complex (elutes first) from small free drug molecules; Hummel-Dreyer variant equilibrates the column with drug.
Other methods: UV/fluorescence spectroscopy (change in spectrum on binding), electrophoresis, circular dichroism, and ion-selective electrodes.
Data from these methods are plotted by Klotz (1/r vs 1/Df) or Scatchard (r/Df vs r) plots to obtain the number of sites (n) and binding constant (K).
Precautions: constant temperature (37°C) and pH 7.4, avoid drug degradation and membrane binding, use physiological protein concentrations.
a.diagram: Equilibrium dialysis cell: two compartments separated by a semipermeable membrane; left compartment with protein (large circles) and drug (dots, some attached to protein); right compartment buffer with free drug dots only; label 'at equilibrium free drug equal on both sides'.
a.conclusion: Accurate measurement of free drug by these methods is the basis of all protein binding calculations.

long.q: Define buffer capacity and derive the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a weak acid and its salt. Discuss the applications of buffers in pharmaceutical systems.
long.hi: pH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]; buffer capacity β = ΔB/ΔpH

kp.t: Buffer capacity β = ΔB/ΔpH (gram equivalents per litre per pH unit)
Assumptions: acid weakly ionised, salt fully ionised
Maximum capacity at pH = pKa (0.576 C)
Applications: stability and solubility of drugs
Low capacity near physiological pH to avoid irritation

a.intro: A buffer resists change in pH on addition of small amounts of acid or alkali. Buffer capacity (β) is the number of gram equivalents of strong acid or base required to change the pH of 1 litre of buffer by one unit: β = ΔB/ΔpH.
points: Weak acid HA ionises: HA + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + A-; Ka = [H3O+][A-]/[HA].
Rearranging: [H3O+] = Ka × [HA]/[A-].
Taking negative logarithms: -log[H3O+] = -log Ka - log([HA]/[A-]), i.e. pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).
Assumptions: the weak acid is very little ionised (especially with common ion from the salt), so [HA] ≈ concentration of acid; the salt is completely ionised, so [A-] ≈ concentration of salt.
Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log [salt]/[acid]. When [salt] = [acid], pH = pKa.
Buffer capacity (Van Slyke): β = 2.303 C Ka[H3O+]/(Ka + [H3O+])²; it is maximum at pH = pKa (βmax = 0.576 C) and increases with total buffer concentration C; useful range pKa ± 1.
Applications - stability: drugs are formulated at the pH of maximum stability (e.g. many esters and penicillins degrade with pH), using buffers such as acetate, citrate, phosphate.
Solubility: buffers keep weak acid/base drugs in solution (e.g. at pH where the ionised form is enough to stay dissolved).

Ophthalmic and parenteral products: pH close to that of tears/blood (about 7.4) and low buffer capacity so body fluids quickly bring them to physiological pH; reduces pain and irritation. Boric acid and phosphate buffers are used for eye drops.

Other uses: analytical work (calibration of pH meters, assays, chromatography mobile phases), dissolution media, microbiological culture media, and preparation of standard buffers (Clark-Lubs, Sorensen phosphate).
a.diagram: Plot of buffer capacity β (y) vs pH (x): bell-shaped curve with maximum at pH = pKa; or titration curve of acetic acid with NaOH showing a flat buffer region around pH 4.76.
a.conclusion: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation lets the formulator prepare a buffer of the required pH, and buffer capacity decides how strongly it holds that pH.

long.q: Explain Sorensen's pH scale. Describe the electrometric determination of pH using the glass electrode and pH meter.
long.hi: Glass electrode + calomel reference; E = E° - 0.0591 pH

kp.t: Glass electrode: thin glass membrane, internal Ag/AgCl in HCl
Potential changes by 0.0591 V per pH unit at 25°C

a.intro: Sorensen (1909) introduced the pH scale to express hydrogen ion concentration conveniently: pH = -log[H+]. Electrometric methods measure pH from the potential of an electrode that responds to hydrogen ions.
points: pH scale: 0 to 14 at 25°C; pH 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 alkaline; pH + pOH = 14. A change of one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H+].
Principle: the potential of a hydrogen-ion-sensitive electrode against a reference electrode follows the Nernst equation: E = E° - 0.0591 pH at 25°C, so the measured EMF is converted to pH.
Hydrogen electrode: platinum black electrode with hydrogen gas at 1 atm; the primary standard, but inconvenient and poisoned by many substances.
Quinhydrone electrode: platinum wire in solution saturated with quinhydrone; simple but not usable above about pH 8 or with oxidising/reducing agents.
Glass electrode: a thin bulb of special pH-sensitive glass containing 0.1 N HCl and an internal Ag/AgCl electrode; potential across the glass membrane depends on [H+] of the test solution.
Reference electrode: saturated calomel electrode (Hg/Hg2Cl2/saturated KCl) or Ag/AgCl, which provides a constant potential; modern instruments use a combined electrode.
pH meter: a high-impedance voltmeter (because glass has very high resistance) with temperature compensation, reading directly in pH units.

Procedure: switch on and stabilise, set temperature, calibrate with two standard buffers (e.g. pH 4.0 and 7.0, or 7.0 and 9.2), rinse electrode with water, dip in sample, read pH; store glass electrode wet.
Advantages: accurate (±0.01-0.02), works for coloured, turbid and oxidising/reducing solutions, small volume.
Limitations: alkaline (sodium) error above about pH 10, acid error below about pH 1, electrode is fragile and needs calibration and hydration.
a.diagram: Draw a pH meter: beaker with test solution, glass electrode (bulb with internal HCl and Ag/AgCl wire) and saturated calomel reference electrode (with KCl and porous plug) dipped in it, both connected to a meter with digital display.
a.conclusion: The glass electrode pH meter is the standard pharmacopoeial method for accurate pH measurement of pharmaceutical products.

long.q: Discuss buffered isotonic solutions. Explain the measurement of tonicity, the Liso value, and the methods (Class I and Class II) for adjusting tonicity.
long.hi: Isotonic = 0.9% NaCl, -0.52°C; cryoscopic, NaCl equivalent, White-Vincent, Sprowls

kp.t: Liso: ΔTf = Liso × c (1.9 non-electrolyte, 3.4 uni-univalent)
Class I: cryoscopic and NaCl equivalent
Class II: White-Vincent (V = w × E × 111.1) and Sprowls

a.intro: Ophthalmic, nasal and parenteral solutions should be isotonic with body fluids and buffered near physiological pH to avoid pain, irritation and tissue damage. Isotonic solutions have the same osmotic pressure as blood and tears (0.9% NaCl, freezing point -0.52°C).
points: Hypotonic solutions cause swelling and haemolysis of RBCs; hypertonic solutions cause shrinking (crenation); both irritate tissues.

Isosmotic vs isotonic: isosmotic solutions have equal osmotic pressure measured physically; isotonic means equal tonicity across a living membrane. 1.9% boric acid is isosmotic with blood but causes haemolysis because boric acid crosses the RBC membrane; it is isotonic with tears.

Measurement of tonicity - haemolytic method: RBCs are suspended in the test solution and observed for swelling/haemolysis (or haemolysis measured spectrophotometrically against standard NaCl solutions).
Colligative method: freezing point depression (cryoscope), vapour pressure or osmotic pressure (osmometer) of the solution is measured and compared with 0.52°C.

Liso value: ΔTf = Liso × c (c = molar concentration); Liso is about 1.9 for non-electrolytes, 2.0 for weak electrolytes, 3.4 for uni-univalent and 4.3 for uni-divalent electrolytes. It allows estimation of ΔTf and E values: E = 17 Liso/M.
Class I methods (add NaCl or other agent to lower freezing point to -0.52°C): Cryoscopic method W = (0.52 - a)/b; sodium chloride equivalent method NaCl needed = 0.9 - Σ(w × E) g per 100 mL.
Class II methods (add water to make the drug isotonic, then dilute with an isotonic vehicle): White-Vincent method V = w × E × 111.1 mL; Sprowls method uses precalculated V values for 0.3 g of drug.
Buffered isotonic vehicles: isotonic phosphate or boric acid buffers are used to make up the volume so the final solution is both isotonic and at the desired pH.
Example: to make 30 mL of 1% drug solution isotonic by White-Vincent: w = 0.3 g, V = 0.3 × E × 111.1 mL water, then add isotonic buffered vehicle to 30 mL.
a.diagram: Draw three RBCs: in isotonic solution (normal biconcave), hypotonic (swollen, bursting with arrows of water entering) and hypertonic (shrunken, crenated, water leaving).
a.conclusion: Correct tonicity and buffering make parenteral and ophthalmic products safe and comfortable.

mcq.explain: Tetracyclines form poorly absorbed chelates with polyvalent metal ions.
